utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start, if I may just mention something? Mr. Wladimiroff is not in court this morning. He is sorting matters out in relation to witness difficulties in Banja Luka. I dare say information will be coming back to the Court shortly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. If there is anything that we can do, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think he knows that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Would you like to continue, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. PROFESSOR ROBERT HAYDEN, recalled. Examined by MR. ORIE, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, you understand you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. You may be seated. Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor Hayden, we finished yesterday by paying attention to Article 135 of the 1990 Serbian Constitution. I would like to present another document to you both in the original language and in a translation. (Handed). Professor Hayden, could you please tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a slightly enlarged photocopy of Serbo-Croatian versions 28 of amendments to the Slovenia Constitution in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document as being Defence Exhibits 48A and B; A for the original language and B for the translation, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibits 48A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if you please would put the English version on the monitor? I would like to draw your attention to Amendment XLVI.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could you tell us what Amendment XLVI deals with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, OK. First, I should say that these were amendments passed, amendments to the Constitution of Slovenia that were passed in September of 1989, and that were the focus of a great deal of discussion throughout Yugoslavia actually in they appear here in a Serbo-Croatian newspaper, the independent newspaper, Borba. What we are looking at is the final version, the final version, of the amendments, the amendments as passed. Amendment XLVI says: "In the course of their activities in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia, the organs of the federation shall respect the constitutional right of the equality of the languages on the part of the members of all the nations and nationalities". The controversial part was the next clause: "If activities or enactments by the organs of the federation violate the 28 constitutional status and rights of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia, the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia shall take measures in accordance with Amendment LXII".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if you would compare this Amendment to the Slovenian Constitution with the provisions of the Serbian constitution, what would be your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would actually have to look first at Amendment LXII which is now in front of us. It says: "If the organs of the federation adopt a decision which is not in accordance with their competence as set out in the Constitution, and thereby infringe on the constitutional status and the rights of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia, the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia shall take measures in order to protect the status and rights of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia as defined in the Constitution." This Amendment, of course, read along with the Amendment before it, is very comparable to the Serbian Amendment -- Serbian Article No. 135 of the Serbian Constitution which was passed a year later. The Serbian Constitution was adopted in September 1990. This Slovenian Constitution was adopted in September of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at these amendments to the Constitutions, both of Serbia and Slovenia, I would like to put to you a quote that I also put to Dr. Gow. It was a quote of a statement he gave in the Foreign Affairs Committee in the House of Commons. Would you agree if I would say that: "It is fair to say that the Slovenes were the first to give up on Yugoslavia", at least if you 28 understand that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would certainly agree with that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please explain why you think that the Slovenes were the "first to give up"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The amendments to the Slovenian Constitution in 1989 were very controversial because they, effectively, negated the principle of supremacy of the federal constitution. In doing so, they threatened the entire constitutional order of Federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, Dr. Gow has expressed as his opinion on 8th May in this Court answering to a question, the question was: "When did the federation of Yugoslavia cease to function?" He opined that the date in which the federation ceased to function was 15th May 1991. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the date is almost two years late. The federation, the Yugoslav federation, well, it began a process of decreasing functionality with the passage of the Slovenian amendments in September of 1989, and specifically the first federal organ to essentially pass into ineffectiveness, an effective nullity, was the constitutional court of Federal Yugoslavia, because there was an attempt made by the federal government (headed by Ante Markovic) to bring the Slovenian amendments before the federal court. The Slovenian government refused to recognise the competence of the federal court to hear the issue, refused to participate in the hearing before the constitutional, the 28 federal constitutional court, which actually did hear the case and rendered a decision which was ignored by the Republic of Slovenia. Over the course of the next year and a half, as it became obvious that a Republic could ignore federal authority and get away with it, increasingly republics ignored federal authority, ignored directives of the federal government and thereby brought the federal structure to a halt. We might say that that process could have been seen, I do not know if we would say it took its ultimate form in May of 1991 or not, by that stage certainly the federal government as an effective federal government had been blocked, particularly in the summer of 1990 and particularly by the efforts of the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Serbia soon to be followed by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, after we discussed the chronology of who was first in not respecting any more the federal authority, I would like to change subjects with you and turn to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one minute, Mr. Orie, if I may interrupt you? What was the date of the ignoring by Slovenia of the decision of the constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was December of 1989. I believe that the court sat in late September or in October of 1989, rendered a decision on the Slovenian Constitution as well on the constitutions of the other republics in December of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So that would be the date then that you would consider that the federal order ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly that was the day at which it became apparent 28 that the federal order would cease to exist because the constitutional court -- the constitutional court was in the constitutional structure as the mechanism for deciding the most important questions of relationships within the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That was ignored by Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, its ability to do so had been destroyed by the unilateral actions of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask this question? I take it that the matter that came before the Court was on the question of the Slovenian Constitution that you have just drawn our attention to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The matter that was before the court had to do with whether or not the Slovenian amendments were contrary to the federal constitution because the federal constitution did have a provision that said that the republican constitutions could not be contrary to the federal constitution and this was the question that was brought to the federal constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I would like to turn now, Professor Hayden, to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina from a constitutional point of view and as far as sovereignty is concerned. Could you explain to us whether there was a different situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as the concept of sovereignty was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1974, as in the rest of Yugoslavia, you would see the dual form of sovereignty that I discussed earlier yesterday. The working people and the working class, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, in Bosnia and Herzegovina 28 the nations -- plural -- narodi, narods, of Bosnia and Herzegovina specified as Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and the nationalities and others, but specified Muslims, Serbs and Croats. This, of course, reflects the situation that in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was no single majority narod.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please explain this to us a bit more in detail looking at the 1974 Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which I will present to you. My first question is whether this is this Constitution. Unfortunately, the English text is in the top and the original text is in the back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the 1974 Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbo-Croatian original is from the same source that the Croatian Constitution was found in yesterday. It is a collection of Constitutions of Yugoslavia and of the Republics, published in Belgrade in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document as Defence Exhibit 49A; A for original language and B for translation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 49A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you could be a bit more specific perhaps on this document on the question just raised about the different situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina as far as the sovereignty was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we look at Article 1 of the 1974 Constitution: "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a socialist democratic state and socialist self-management democratic 28 community of working people and citizens, the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Muslims Serbs and Croats", this type of formulation is what we had found in the federal Constitution of '74, "the working people and citizens and the nations and nationalities", but here the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the nations are specified, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, based on the usual formulations, "the power and self-management of the working class and all working people and on the sovereignty and equality of the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina", etc. Then: "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a component of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia". You see a similar idea expressed in Article 2: "Working people and citizens, the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Serbs, Croats and Muslims and members of other nations and nationalities, realise their sovereign rights in the Socialist Republic". Article 3: "In the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the equality of the nations and nationalities and their members is guaranteed".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us about rules on the proportional representation under this Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually if we continue with Article 3 at the bottom of the page, this has to do that the Article is on the equality of the nations and nationalities, "Conditions for the affirmation of national values" etc. "as well as proportional representation in the assemblies of social-political organisations, are ensured for the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Croats, Muslims and Serbs and members of other nations and nationalities". 28 "Proportional representation in the assemblies" is a constitutional requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the structure, the constitutional structure, as far as sovereignty and equal representation, subsequently changed in Bosnia and Herzegovina? I might present an exhibit to you and would ask you what these documents are. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbo-Croatian is a photocopy of the Official Gazette, the Sluzbenilist, of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 31st July 1990, and it contains Amendments L1X to LXXX on the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender these documents as Defence Exhibit 50A for the original language and 50B for the translation, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibits 50A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like you to look first at Amendment LX. Could you please explain what changes to the 1974 Constitutions were adopted in Amendment LX?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the amendments, of course, were passed in July 1990 and, as with the other essentially post socialist amendments, you will see that the workers, the working people and working class have been deleted from the constitutional structure. So that in place of Article 1 of the Constitution of 1974 that we saw in the last exhibit, we now have that "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a democratic sovereign state of equal 28 citizens, the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Muslims, Serbs and Croats and the members of the other nations and nationalities living in it".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So is it right, am I understanding, that different from what happened in the other republics, that in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was no majority people that, well, if I could say, took over as the primary one in the Constitution and that all the peoples, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, were equal under this new Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the constitutional structure. There is no single majority narod in the Yugoslav sense. You cannot then have a parallel to the Slovenian declaration or the Croatian declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, were there any changes in the system of proportional representation under these new amendments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the following Amendment, Amendment LX1, replaces the previous Article 3 and now says: "In the assemblies of social and political associations, the organs which they elect, the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and other state organs, proportionate representation of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be ensured". Now, what this does is make the requirement of proportionality much more inclusive. It now includes the presidency. Bosnia and Herzegovina, like the Yugoslav federation of which it was still a part, did not have a single President of the Republic. It had a group, a presidency, a 28 collective presidency, of which there would be a President of the presidency who was regarded as being the first among equals. In principle, the presidency would take decisions and the President of the presidency would issue them in the name of the presidency. This Amendment requires proportional representation in the presidency as well as in state organs, social-political associations -- in other words, throughout the governmental structures of Bosnia and Herzegovina proportional representation is to be ensured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, strict proportionality might be a bit difficulty in practice. Could you tell us whether any deviation from this strict proportionality was permitted under the Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it is under the -- in the same exhibit and Yugoslav Constitutions were always accompanied by a constitutional law for the implementation of the Constitution, always. I have never been clear, being an American lawyer, as to why this is necessary, but there is always a constitutional law for the implementation. We find the translation of this in the last several pages of this exhibit. The original is also in this exhibit because the constitutional law followed in the Official Gazette directly on the text of the Amendment. So if we look at ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put it on the screen so we can look at the document, Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. What we will see here is the constitutional law for the 28 implementation of these amendments and Article 19 here: "For the purpose of implementing Amendment LX1, it shall be considered that proportionate representation of the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Muslims, Serbs and Croats -- in social and political associations is ensured if the proportion does not deviate by more than 15 per cent from the proportion determined". You will see that the proportions are to be determined on the basis of data from the census before the elections. As one carries through this Article of the Constitutional law, it is fairly specific as to what is to be done in regard to the nationalities and other minorities as well. So that they are clearly taking this requirement of proportionality quite seriously in these amendements in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, Professor Hayden, having looked at this very precise rule on proportional representation, whether any mechanism was created to safeguard, to respect, for the proportional representation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am not sure if I would say it would -- certainly there is an electoral committee -- I think we will see that later -- which ensures in elections that the principle proportionality is met in the elections. There was also within these same Amendments an Amendment that was there to ensure equality of the nations by preventing, as they put it, outvoting on critical issues. In other words, there is a provision, an amendment, that sets up a council on national equality. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I was asking for the mechanism, organs, 28 created, whenever any dispute would arise on this issue, on how they would solve the issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. If we turn to the amendments, back to the amendments within this Exhibit, Amendment LXX on page, beginning on page 2 of the translation, what is particularly important is clause 10 of Amendment LXX, which is a long and, as you will see, complicated clause, and in the best tradition of Yugoslav Constitutionalism it is sometimes hard to interpret in the original, much less in translation. However, this is within the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina: "A Council on the Questions of Ensuring the Equality of the Nations and Nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be established in the Assembly ... An equal number of deputies from the members of nations of ... Muslims, Serbs and Croats, a corresponding number of deputies from among other nations and nationalities and others who live in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be elected as members of the Council. The Council shall make decisions on the basis of consent of the members representing all the nations and nationalities". This is a requirement of consensus. "The composition, scope and manner of activities of the Council shall be determined by a law which shall be passed with a two-thirds majority of the total number of deputies". Then it provides that, "The Council shall give special attention to matters relating to: the equality of languages and alphabets", and etc., "the organisation and activities of cultural institutions and the institutions of special importance 28 for expression and affirmation of the national characteristics of individual nations ... and passing regulations in order to ensure the implementation of constitutional provisions, which explicitly set out the principles of the equality of nations and nationalities". It then says that, "This Council shall be obliged to consider the issue of the equality of nations and nationalities following an initiative by the deputies in the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If no fewer than 20 deputies deem that a proposed regulation or other act within the jurisdiction of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina undermines the equality of nations and nationalities, the proposal being discussed by the Assembly ... shall be formulated by the Council". What this means is that if a minimum of 20 deputies refer an issue to this Council, the Council will then formulate the question as it will then be discussed by the Assembly. In other words, for the Assembly to discuss the question it will have to be in the form in which the question is referred back to the Assembly by this Council which has to act on the basis of unanimity. Further: "On a proposal by the Council, the Assembly ... shall make decisions ... in accordance with the special procedure set out in the Rules of Procedure ... by a two-thirds majority of the total number of deputies".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, after having heard this mechanism of unanimity the commission and then putting it to Parliament and requiring a 28 two-thirds majority to adopt any decision on these issues, these are all very much details. Could you please summarise -- really summarise and make it short -- the major changes, just in brief, so that we have a survey of what we discussed more in detail a second ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I mean, a major change is that the working class and all working people are expelled from the Constitution leaving the nations as a kind of partitioned sovereign, partitioned into segments which are then guaranteed proportional representation in the organs and in the Assembly and in the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This mechanism is set up to ensure that the Assembly, the Parliament, cannot take measures against the will, effectively, of one of these component sovereigns, one of the components of this group sovereign in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like now to go with you to what happened actually in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can I ask just one more question regarding these amendments?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are there any amendments in 1990 of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Constitution that speak to the primacy of the federal Constitution, as were the amendments in Slovenia, Croatia and Serbia? Are there any amendments that speak about the relationship between the Republic and the Constitution and the federal Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so at this time. I do not remember that there 28 was such an amendment in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, after these Amendments were adopted, were elections held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the elections, the first until now only free and fair elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina since the end of the communism, were held in November of 1990. These Amendments had been passed in July of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like to give two documents to you and could you please tell us what these documents are about? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbo-Croatian original is a photocopy of the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sluzbenilist, Bosnia and Herzegovina, from 19th December 1990; and it is a report by the Republican Electoral Commission about the results of the elections of 1990, November 1990. Then there is a translation of parts of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender these documents, your Honours, as Defence Exhibit 51A for the original language and 51B for the translation in English.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence Exhibits 51A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if you just could give us a brief idea of how this document is structured, not going through it in all detail, but just to give us an impression of what is in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We will not go through it in full detail. It begins 28 simply with a brief explanation of what it is, that these are the results of the election. It then lists -- most of this document consists of lists of the results of the elections. It is in Cyrillic, of course, but it says: "The results of the election by electoral unit". This part of it is not translated which is why I am just pointing it out on the screen here. Then this happens to be the electoral unit constituency of Banja Luka. Then what it does is it lists the total number of registered voters, in this case 552,576, of which 433,226 voted. They elected 25 members of the parliament here and these were elected by lists of the various parties. So it lists the Democratic Socialist League of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 14,000 votes, won a position. Then it goes down for the various electoral units here. This is for the Council of Citizens of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It then, and I believe I can then switch -- well, perhaps I should do one other thing. There are two Chambers in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly and I trust that the translators -- well, maybe you are trusting my translation here. If you look to the other Chamber which did elect individuals, we happen again to have Banja Luka and similar -- and we have figures on voters. These are actually smaller districts, obviously, because you have 136,000. Then it lists each candidate, Nikola Erceg, Serb, Banja Luka, that is where he is from, a candidate of the Serbian Democratic Party of 28 Bosnia-Herzegovina who received 52,000 votes; here you have the next one, Obrad Milidrag, Serb, from another Party, received 3,000 votes; Dr. Anto Cosic, Croat, from his Party, the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, received 11,000 votes; Ivica Bijelic Croat, from the League of Reform Parties of Yugoslavia, received 14,000 votes; Dzevad -- I cannot read it clearly -- Osmancevic, I think, Muslim, a Muslim from Banja Luka, candidate of the League of Communists and the Social Democratic Party and the Democratic Socialists; Salahudin Mesanovic, a Muslim. So then what you see is that each candidate is identified by Party and by narod, and almost everyone is identified as a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim, although occasionally there is a Yugoslav in there, and I think occasionally there are one or two other identifications but primarily Serb, Croat and Muslims. This is simply the way it is reported by the Electoral Commission. The Electoral Commission then, as part of its report -- here we can turn to the translation -- did a breakdown of the ethnic composition or the national composition of the deputies elected. Here you see Muslims -- to the Citizens Chamber, Citizens Council, Muslims 56, Serbs 45, Croats 25, Yugoslavs 4. Then it looks at the ethnic composition of the Republic, according to the 1981 census -- that was the most recent census -- and gives you a range of deputies and eventually pronounces that the breakdown that was actually achieved in the elections was adequate. It does a report on 28 this. Adequate proportionate ethnic representation of the deputies, according to Articles 19 to 22 of the Constitutional law that we looked at. So it goes through all this and then proclaims, it shows you what the range could be, and then proclaims the results actually to be within that range and eventually says that adequate proportionate ethnic representation has been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if I could ask you to describe any recognisable pattern in the outcome of these elections, how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In these elections in November 1990, which were done -- international observers were present and proclaimed them to be free and fair, the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina did have the opportunity to vote for a non-communist Party headed by the most popular political figure in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time and, in fact, throughout Yugoslavia at the time, who stood for a state of equal citizens, a civil society of equal citizens. About six per cent of them did so. Overwhelmingly, the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina voted as Serbs, Muslims and Croats, Serbs voting overwhelmingly for the Serbian Democratic Party, a single Party; Croats voting overwhelmingly for the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ; Muslims voting overwhelmingly for the single Muslim Party, the Party of the Stranka Demokraske Akcije Party, of Democratic Action, SDA. The percentages of votes for each of these national 28 parties is slightly under that nations' narods' proportionality in the census of 1981 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand well that the outcome of the elections was mainly according to the ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The election almost amounted to a census, an ethnic census of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, from an historical point of view, was this a surprise? If you had compared the outcome of this election with earlier elections, for example, in this century, could you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There have not been too many relatively free and fair elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina in this century. However, there were such elections in, I believe, 1910 in the Austro-Hungarian Empire and in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in the 1920s. The results were very similar to the results of the 1990 election with Serbs voting overwhelmingly for one Serb Party, Croats overwhelmingly for one Croat Party, Muslims overwhelmingly for one Muslim Party. So these results were very comparable to earlier .....

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden could you tell us how then a government was formed after these elections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask a question just before that? I had gained the impression that that this election resulted in a surprise in one sense because the Serb proportion had fallen to less than the Muslim proportion or am I thinking only of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you may be thinking of Prijedor and I am not 28 familiar with the specific results in the local election in Prijedor. I could say -- I actually do not know the basis of your question -- I would only say that -- I said yesterday, I believe, that Muslims were granted the status of a narod, of a nation, in 1971, and immediately the number of Muslims increased, the people who declared themselves as Muslims, the number of Serbs dropped. It has to do with the advantages and disadvantages of declaring oneself what one is, but I am not sure if that is the basis of your question. I suppose I should leave it alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Do not trouble. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, then I will repeat my question, how then was a government formed after these elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After these elections, the leaders of the three winning parties, because the other parties were purely marginal, in other words, the leaders of the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, worked out an arrangement in which they would share power. The Bosnia and Herzegovina, like Yugoslavia, like most of the Republics, had a structure of government. As I said, there was a collective presidency. There was a Parliament, an Assembly, and then there was a government, essentially an administration. The deal worked out was that there would, of course, be seven members of the presidency -- this was constitutionally provided -- two Serbs, two Croats, two Muslims and a man who was elected as a Yugoslav. Actually, I think the results of that election may even be in this exhibit. It was agreed among them that a Muslim politician, Alija Izetbegovic, would become 28 President of the presidency, to be first among equals in the presidency. He had not actually received the highest number of votes of the SDA politicians and other Muslim politicians had received a higher number of votes, but Alija Izetbegovic was to be President of the presidency. A Serb politician, Momcilo Krajisnik, from the SDS was made President Speaker of the Assembly, President of the Parliament, and a Croatian politician, Ure Pelivan, who was made President of the administration of the government. These terms were to last for two years and then they were to rotate. I believe a Croat, for example, was supposed to become President of the presidency after two years, which in fact never happened. But, in any event, then within the administration, within the government, the government was headed by Mr. Pelivan, President of the government or, perhaps, Prime Minister would be an equivalent position. There were, I believe, 22 ministries in the Bosnia and Herzegovina government. 10 portfolios were given to Muslims to head, seven to Serbs and five to Croats. So this was a package, a deal, by which a Muslim became President of the presidency, a Serb President of the Parliament, and a Croat President of the government of the administration. As I said, these positions were supposed to rotate at the end of two years. They came into effect in December 1990 and were supposed to rotate at the end of two years. You may recall that the President, the presidency of the presidency of Federal Yugoslavia also rotated. This is when 28 Dr. Gow said that Federal Yugoslavia ceased to exist when a rotation was blocked, so this was not unprecedented in Yugoslav constitutional structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did the rotation work as foreseen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the positions never did rotate. Of course, they would have rotated in December of 1992 and the war broke out in April and May of 1992. However, it was all quite curious. As I said, a Croat was supposed to rotate into the position of President of the presidency in December 1992, and even though the Croatian Democratic Union did not officially pronounce secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the relations between Croatian and Muslim politicians were strained at that time. So that we had the very curious situation in, I believe, February 1993 when the President of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who was a Croat, was writing to inform the United States, the United Nations, that Mr. Izetbegovic was actually not legitimately President of the presidency because his term had expired and that he was still a member of the presidency but was not legitimately President of the presidency. Now, that issue has essentially vanished and, in fact, most of the people regard Mr. Izetbegovic as President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although that is not actually a position that is provided for in the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, after having gone through the theory of the Constitution and how it was practised, I would like to take you to a subsequent stage of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would first like to present to you a document. Could you 28 please tell us what document that is? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is opinion No. 1 of the Badinter Commission, the European Communities Arbitration Commission, the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia. The source is a volume by Shezana Trifunovska, "Yugoslavia Through Documents", published in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour, as Defence Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 52 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could you explain to us how a state was defined in this first Badinter opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this opinion had to do with the status, essentially, of Federal Yugoslavia as it still existed at this stage. You can see that the President of the Arbitration Committee received the letter from Lord Carrington in November 1991. The question was, essentially, what would be the status of Federal Yugoslavia considering the events that had taken place, the pronounced secessions of Slovenia and Croatia and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the definition of a state is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Badinter Commission began by defining the state in 1(B) here: "The State is commonly defined as a community which consists of a territory and a population subject to an organised political authority".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, would you accept the view given by the Badinter Commission in its opinion that it is necessary to take into consideration the form of internal political organisation 28 and the constitutional provisions in order to determine the government's sway over the population and the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that is absolutely necessary. Also, if we are defining the state as in part one of the criteria is a population subject to an organised political authority, the Constitution would seem to be the instrument that provides the organisation of political authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In applying these criteria, what was the conclusion of the Badinter Committee in regard to the federation? I am not talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, but about a federation in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conclusion of the Commission -- if I can find it here; it is here -- they noted that various of the republics had withdrawn their representatives from the organs of the federation. Then it said that these organs of the federation no longer meet the criteria of participation and representativeness inherent in a federal State. They noted the recourse to force has led to armed conflict, that the authorities of the federation and the Republics have shown themselves powerless to do anything about it. The Arbitration Committee came to the conclusion that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was at the time in the process of dissolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, by applying these criteria to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the end of 1991, beginning of 1992, could you please tell us what your opinion is about the statehood of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that period of time? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina entered a period of constitutional breakdown and, in Badinter terms, of dissolution beginning in October of 1991 and I would imagine more or less concluding at the end of January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like to go with you in more detail about this period of time. Could you tell us what events led to the breakdown of the constitutional structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that period of time, and would you also tell us about the chronology of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina functioned with this essential coalition government, essentially a coalition government, until October of -- until the middle of October in 1991 when the political agreements, the political consensus, that made this coalition possible broke down in the course of a parliamentary session in the middle of October, October 14th and 15th, of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like to present to you Prosecution Exhibit 47. (Handed). Could you just in order to refresh our memories tell us what Exhibit 47 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, Exhibit 47 is a photocopy of an article from Yugoslav Survey called "The Platform on the Position of Bosnia and Herzegovina and The Future Organisation of the Yugoslav Community". Now what this is is a -- it is a representation, it is a reproduction, of a declaration of sovereignty that was the subject of quite a lot of debate in the Bosnian Parliament, the Bosnian Assembly, on October 14th and 15th of 1991, and it was a very dramatic occasion. I believe that you saw very, very short segments of film in the course of Dr. Gow's testimony and 28 slightly more in the course of the cross-examination of Dr. Gow of some of the parliamentary speeches at this time. The events focused around what was called a Memorandum or letter of intent and a Platform -- if this could somehow be brought in so I can, well, all right -- Memorandum, letter of intent and a Platform on the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the future organisation of the Yugoslav Community that were presented to the Parliament, to the Assembly, by the SDA, the Muslim Party, with the support of the HDZ, the Croatian Party, in the Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like you, Professor Hayden, to take us to clause 2 of this Memorandum and explain to us what the meaning of it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clause 2 of the Memorandum, yes, OK, here. Now, at this time, in October of 1991, Slovenia and Croatia had seceded and a war is going on in Croatia. You see here that the position stated in this Memorandum is that, "Bosnia and Herzegovina will continue to strive for the survival of the Yugoslav community on new and ever more acceptable bases. In the meantime, it will also endeavour to promote the normal functioning of existing common institutions, but its representatives will not attend the meetings of the Assembly and of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, if the latter are not attended by representatives of all the republics and provinces. Bosnia and Herzegovina will not be bound by any decisions taken by these bodies while they are incomplete". So, what it says is, while it formally announces support for the continuing existence of Yugoslavia and for the 28 normal functioning of its institutions, it will -- it says that Bosnia will not take part in these institutions because it is very clear that the Slovenes and the Croats will not, and so it is very clear that Bosnia will not either which is an interesting form of support.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like you to take us now to clauses 5 and 6, Professor Hayden, to see what is in there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. "The positions set out in this memorandum express the will of the majority of this Assembly and, as such, the political will of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina; consequently, they constitute an obligatory basis for the conduct of the state and political bodies of the Republic. "Proceeding from the right of the parliamentary majority to decide on the fate of the Republic as a whole, this Assembly recognises, simultaneously, the right of the parliamentary minority to claim and realise every one of its legitimate interests ... provided this is achieved without use of force and in a legal and democratic manner".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like you to take us to the Platform and tell us what this is, what it contains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Platform is a statement of the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia, and it is interesting for any number of reasons. One of them, however, is the second clause in paragraph 1, that "any possibility of outvoting in the process of decision-making on crucial issues concerning the equal rights of all nations and nationalities living in the Republic will be precluded through an appropriate structure of the Assembly of 28 Bosnia and Herzegovina".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: This rather ambiguous document, was it opposed by any other document at that time, and may I please present to you ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can just ask, does that not really mean complete stalemate? There cannot be any outvoting, it should be precluded in some way; so that if you have any dissent, nothing is accomplished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would read that as a reference to the same type of mechanism that was included in this Amendment LXX, clause 10, of the Bosnian Constitution which was then still valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That there must be consensus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that if at least 20 members of parliament referred an issue to this Council on national equality, the question would have -- for further consideration by the Assembly, the question would have to be formulated by unanimous consent of this Council on national equality. This was the valid amendment to the then existing Constitution. One could say that these paragraphs 5 and 6 of the Memorandum, of the letter of intent, express something that is contrary to amendment LXX, clause 10. The position set out in this Memorandum expressed the will of the majority of this Assembly and as such the political will of the citizens, and refers to the right of the parliamentary majority to decide on the fate of the Republic as a whole, which sounds fine except that Amendment LXX, clause 10, has provided a mechanism by which for particular types of questions this would have to be done. One will recall that when the issue comes out of this Council on national equality, it must still be passed by 28 a special two-thirds majority, not by a simple majority, of the Assembly. So that the sensitive questions, questions that one of the constituent nations regards as sensitive, must be passed at a minimum. Even if one were to bypass the Council procedures which could still stalemate, you would still see an intent that such issues be passed by a two-thirds majority of the parliament, not a simple majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: This, Dr. Hayden, was proposed by two of the three Parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was proposed by the Muslim Party, the SDA, and it was supported by the HDZ, the Croatian Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to present to you another document, Professor Hayden, and would you please tell us what these are? It is again an A and a B version? I would like you in the first document to look at the right bottom corner of the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. The document, as a whole, is a photocopy of the first and second and third pages of the independent Belgrade newspaper, Borba, the issue of 16th October. Although it does not actually say it on the cover page, it is actually 16th October 1991. It does say that on page 2. The part to which you refer is a box of text in the lower right-hand corner of page 2. The translation here is the translation of this lower right-hand corner of page 2 entitled: "Resolution on the position of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis by the SDS", by the Serbian Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour, as Defence Exhibit 28 53A for the original language and B for the portion translated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibits 53A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, was this a competing document compared to the Memorandum we were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a competing document presented by the SDS, the Serbian Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps compare this document with the document we just saw as Exhibit 47?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should have kept 47, perhaps, but one sees that the Serbian position is that, "The state of Bosnia and Herzegovina will as a constituent part of the federal state of Yugoslavia respect its constitutional order and its legal system ... and also the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its legal system. "The existing position of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the SFRY will not be changed until the arrival of the conditions from point 3 [sic] of this Resolution". The Resolution does not make any sense if you look at point 3; I suspect they meant point 4. You see that, "Bosnia and Herzegovina will provide the conditions for the uninhibited work of all of its representatives in organs of the Federal State", which is of course in flat contradiction to the Muslim, the Croat proposal. "In federal organs, all of its representatives are required to defend the interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an equal unit 28 of the Federal State, and the equality of all of its nations". The Muslim/Croat Platform, effectively, withdraws representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina from federal organs. Similarly, clause 2: "Bosnia and Herzegovina will support via its organs and its representatives in the organs of the SFRY the maintenance of Yugoslavia", the usual, nice phrasing based on full equality, etc. etc. "It will similarly support changes in the constitutional organ of the Federal State in accordance with the expressed needs and demands and changes which will guarantee the full equality of the six constitutive nations". Clause 3: "Bosnia and Herzegovina will support the continuation of Yugoslavia as the state of all six nations and republics". Then clause 4: "If Croatia secedes from the SFRY and obtains international legal recognition", which had not happened at this stage; Croatia had not be recognised, "then there will be applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina a mechanism for the realisation of the right to self-determination up to secession" -- they quote the 74 federal preamble, without quotation marks, it is the same wording -- "of the constituent nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Muslims, Serbs and Croats) who not wish to remain in such a federal state and wish to organise their own state or to join different international legal recognised states. "The mechanism for realising the right of the nation to self-determination up to secession will be agreed upon by a special act on the plebescite of the constituent nations of 28 Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs, Croats and Muslims with confirmed results of the plebiscite of the nation on the level of each nation, on the level of the entire republic and on the territorial principle", from small to larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Would you, please, Professor Hayden, summarise if possible in a few words what exactly was the difference between these two points of view laid down in the Memorandum on the one hand side and this position paper on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the one primary difference is that by this position Bosnia and Herzegovina would continue to take part in the activities of federal bodies; whereas by the Croat/Muslim position it will not. Another is this clause 4, that if Croatia secedes, then a mechanism for the realisation of the right of self-determination of the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the right to self-determination of the narod -- that constitutional expression of Yugoslavia -- will then be realised within Bosnia and Herzegovina of the individual constituent narods, patterned after the example set by Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What happened then with these competing positions? How was this problem solved, Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was, as I said, a very dramatic occasion and, if you remember the film clips, there was a lot of jeering and applause at different times. It was a parliamentary session that lasted for something like 27 hours on 14th and 15th October in 1991, and it proved not to be possible within the parliament itself to reach a compromise between these two positions, although there were people who attempted to do so, particularly members of 28 those smaller Parties that had been elected as well. There were a few representatives not of these three major Parties. The Serb Party, the SDS, then demanded that this question be put to the Council for questions of national equality which, apparently, had never until that time actually been formed, but they did demand that this be put to the Council for national equality. After, as I say, this very protracted and very, how should one say, excited parliamentary session in the middle of the night on October 15th of 1991, the President of the Parliament, Mr. Krajisnik, who was President of the Parliament as part of the deal that had made Mr. Izetbegovic President of the presidency and Mr. Pelivan President of the Government, a Speaker of the House, President of the Parliament, adjourned the parliamentary session. However, a Muslim member of the Parliament then took the podium and proclaimed a one hour pause. At the end of the hour, the Muslim and Croat representatives came back into the Assembly and voted to accept the SDA's Memorandum by a vote of, I believe, 142 for, none against. There were 240 members of the Parliament. Thus, two-thirds would have required 160 which was not met here. The Serbian representatives regarded this purported (in their terms) parliamentary adoption of the Memorandum as being unconstitutional, in violation of the Constitution, and refused at that moment to take part in the further work of the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They said that until this decision was renounced -- they took, essentially, the same 28 position that the Croat/Muslim Memorandum took in regard to Federal Yugoslavia. The Serbs said, "Look, we are all in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but until this decision, which we regard as unconstitutional, is renounced, we will not take part in the activities of Republican organs". At that stage, the Parliament, which had been operating as normally as such a divided Parliament might be expected to operate, almost ceased to operate normally, as did the Republican organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So the Serb representatives were stepping back, not accepting this decision. You refer to a Muslim member in Parliament proclaiming a one hour pause instead of the adjournment announced by the President of the Parliament, a Serb. Could you tell us what his competence was to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have no idea what his competence would have been to have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, we have discussed now the adoption of the Memorandum, the voting, the way it went in Parliament, rather chaotic. Could you tell us what then actually happened? The Serbs had said that they would not participate any more. Was that the situation? Did they not participate in the functioning of the state organs on from that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not think you mean the Serbs would not participate, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs took the same position in regard to Republican organs in Bosnia that the Muslims were taking in regard to federal organs of Yugoslavia; so, yes, if we are 28 talking about Bosnia, yes, it was the Serbs who were taking this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask, if I may, one question? One fact, I think, has been left out, you alluded to it, but I would like to find out the date that it occurred. When did the President on the federal level refuse to rotate? As I understand it, there was a three person -- no, more than that -- presidency and they were to rotate, and at some point the President -- was he from Montenegro -- refused to rotate as was required by the federal Constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did that not precede the secession of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- yes, it preceded it by approximately one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So what you have then is you have in 1989, I gather, amendments to the Croatian Constitution refusing to recognise the primacy of the federal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Slovenian Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Slovenian, yes. 1990, Croatia, essentially, doing the same thing. 1990, Serbia, though, I gather its amendments did recognise the primacy of the federal Constitution. The next event, I suppose, would be a failure on the part of the President to rotate on the federal level, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are major highlights. Throughout this period ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: There were so many things going on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- what happens after December of 89 when it is clear that the federal constitutional court may safely be ignored ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that. 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- that you have a whole range of activities by various Republics of ignoring federal authority, there was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, I am not ascribing any responsibility, but who held the position of presidency on the federal level and from what Republic ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- when it was not rotated as required?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. That was Borisav Yovic of Serbia who was to be seceded by Stipe Mesic of Croatia, which actually eventually did happen after a period of hesitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But the Serbian President refused to rotate, Slovenia then secedes, Croatia then secedes, Bosnia and Herzegovina in its Constitution did not or at least you could not point us to any amendments that challenge the primacy of the federal Constitution, as did Slovenia's and Croatia's Constitutions. Instead, what they did, after Slovenia and Croatia seceded, was to adopt this Resolution in October, 14th and 15th of 1991, saying, "We will not participate on the federal government level", and at that point in time what had happened was that the presidency of the federal government was being held by a President who should have left, who should have been seceded by another President, according to federal Constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, your Honour, not quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: OK, tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because although Mr. Yovic did step down as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The President of Serbia? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The President from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When did his term expire? I believe it was May of '91, beginning of May '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That was after Slovenia and Croatia seceded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they secede a little bit later. Then there is a period in which the Serbs refuse to confirm Mr. Mesic as the new President of the presidency. However, under a great deal of international pressure they eventually do confirm Mr. Mesic as President of the presidency. So we have this very curious situation that at the time that Croatia and Slovenia secede, actually Mr. Mesic from Croatia is President of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: He had assumed ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He assumed the position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- that position. Do you know the dates, approximate dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I mean, all of this is taking place in May and June of 1991 and, as you can see, it is a very messy situation from all aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When did war break out between Croatia and Serbia then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The greatest hostilities broke out in the summer and fall of 1991. The secessions are not immediately followed by war in Croatia. There is a period in which Croatia has proclaimed itself, has seceded, but the federal army is staying in its barracks and the federal army then is actually trapped within its barracks in many places in Croatia. So you have this whole summer of 1991 in which it is kind of like the period of the phoney war in 1939 after Germany invades Poland and Britain and 28 France declare war but nobody does much of anything until 1940. You have this brief period in the summer of 91 where there is not much conflict. There is the 10 day war in Slovenia. Then there is this eerie period before wide hostilities break out in Croatia in the late summer and the fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When did Slovenia secede then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The secessions are at the end of May, I believe, of '91 and then Croatia at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Which was the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor Hayden, we finished where you explained to us how the adopting of the Memorandum was not constitutional because they did not follow the mechanism for ensuring the protection of the equality of the component nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that the subsequent voting requiring a two-third majority in Parliament was not followed. Could you please tell us whether the adoption of the Memorandum was in line with all the provisions of the Platform you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would actually like to have the Platform back, if I may? It may not be that important. It is OK. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It was Exhibit 47.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 47.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I am waiting for that, I need to clarify something. In one of those inexplicable lapses which makes one cringe, when I was asked when the war broke out, for some reason I said the end of May when the secessions took place. It was the end of June. Why I should have said that, I have not the faintest idea. Well, actually, this was not the Exhibit. However, you will remember the Platform adopted by the Croats and the Muslims in the second clause of the first paragraph said that a mechanism would be created to preclude outvoting on questions of interest or questions relating to the equality of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina which, in response from a question from, I think, Judge Stephen, I said was comparable to seemingly an intent to Amendment LXX, clause 10, of 1990. So it seems that the amendment -- that the Memorandum and the Platform were passed in contravention to Amendment LXX, clause 10, and also in contravention to the provision in the Platform itself that such things would not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if October 1991 marked the beginning of the dissolution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you tell us what marked the final stage of dissolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dissolution, in the sense in which Badinter uses the term, I would say probably the end of January of 1992 when the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina fractured completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to show to you Prosecution Exhibit 52, Professor 28 Hayden, and put some questions in relation to that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I, while we are waiting for that, just ask you a question? There is really no division that ever seems to occur between Bosnia, on the one hand, and Herzegovina on the other. I know writing it out many times it becomes irritating that it is such a long name, but in fact there does not seem to be much geographical or ethnic division between the two, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reasons for the names are primarily historical. There is some linguistic difference. The dialects spoken in Herzegovina are somewhat different from those spoken in Bosnia. There is now quite a bit of a political difference as well -- I suppose there always was, in a sense. The part of Herzegovina called Western Herzegovina, which is where Mostar is located, that was a heavily Croatian area before this war began. It is now exclusively Croatian. The Croatian politicians from Herzegovina, as opposed to Croatian politicians from Bosnia, never hid their intent to have Herzegovina secede from Bosnia and adhere to Croatia. They were the ones who were instrumental in proclaiming the Croation community of Herceg-Bosna. That was in sharp distinction to Croatian politicians from Bosnia itself. So there are some differences that are much more apparent to people from Yugoslavia than they are to the rest of us, including to me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They were not separate nations at one point way back in history, Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would hesitate to say much about Bosnian history because I am not an historian. I am a cultural anthropologist, and I tend to 28 deal with the people as they exist now. I have read a certain amount of history of that part of the world. What can we say, that the peoples who speak Serbo-Croatian are all Slavs linguistically, Slavic peoples of Slavic language families, people who speak the Slavic languages. The history of the region has been such, Empires have come and gone and left their marks, so that the territory of the south Slavs, Yugoslavia -- "Yug" means "south", "Slavia", "of the south Slavs". Parts of it have been ruled by different Empires leaving enormous traces behind and sometimes smaller, and you can even find traces of Napoleon's brief occupation of parts of Croatia if one looks hard enough. For these historical reasons, the peoples have been divided by religion and by script and, hence, divide themselves into these narods that I was discussing yesterday. They distinguish themselves as being different, but the categories are not racial categories certainly, in American terms. The categories are closer, as I have said, to American ethnic groups, but they are very real to the people there. I mean, they know who are Serbs, they know who are Croats, they know who are Muslims. There are differences in customs, in religious practices and sometimes in diet, sometimes in dress, particularly in rural areas. I do not know if I am clarifying this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I asked you to be shown Exhibit 52, Prosecution Exhibit 52, to you. Is that the Badinter 4 opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is opinion No. 4 of the Badinter Commission. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the Badinter Committee dealt with the opposing positions taken by the different parties as we just discussed them before the break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question here to Badinter -- I can look at it here if it is here -- right, so the question here has to do with the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and whether that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be recognised as an independent state by the members of the European Community. So, Badinter goes through the materials that were presented to it, including, as you will see, the Memorandum, item 3, the Memorandum and Platform of the Assembly. Well, obviously the document is fairly lengthy and I do not wish to go through it ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you would take us to the conclusion based upon the presentation of all this information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Badinter did note that -- one can see this at the bottom of the page -- although the Memorandum and the Platform had been passed, right above paragraph 4 here they say: "Outside the institutional framework of SRBH, the 'Serbian people' ... voted in a plebiscite for a 'common Yugoslav state' and passed a Resolution", and they note then that -- they note in several places in this document that Serbian representatives dispute the position taken by the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and they disputed it within the presidency. So, the conclusion in paragraph 4 is that: "In these circumstances, the Arbitration Commission is of the opinion that the will of the peoples", and you will note the plural, "of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute the Socialist Republic of 28 Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to have been fully established".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, did they then require a referendum to be held in order to clarify the existing uncertainty on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One often hears that they required a referendum to be held but, if one looks at the decision, it is a bit more tentative than that. They say that this assessment, that the will of the peoples -- peoples -- cannot be held to have been fully established, but "this assessment could be reviewed ... possibly by means of a referendum", possibly by means of a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like you to go to paragraph 3(b) of the fourth opinion of the Badinter Committee. We see there that a reference is made to Amendment LXVII. Could you please comment on this reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It says -- they actually cite this later on in regard to referenda. This is a citation to Amendment LXVII, it says: "Under the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina ... the citizens exercise their powers through a representative Assembly or by referendum".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Hayden, I would like to present a document to you. Would you please tell us what it is. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an English language translation of Amendment LXVIII to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would it be possible to obtain again the original, the Exhibit of the Amendments to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The original was Defence Exhibit 49A, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you -- no, this is the Constitution of 1974. 28 I need the Constitutional Amendments of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I thought it was 49A and B, but I have become less certain now, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think this is 50A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It might be then our administration is not fully correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You want the amendments to the July 30th 1990 Amendments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is 50A -- 50B if you want to read it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The problem, your Honour, is actually that part of it, Amendments LXVII and LXVIII, are not actually translated into English. The difficulty is that Badinter here -- I assume it is a typographical error because it is not Amendment LXVII. Amendment LXVII deals with funding medical facilities and the like, and so the relevant Amendment is LXVIII. It might be best if I put it ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will first tender the translation of LXVIII as I have offered it to Professor Hayden as Defence Exhibit 54, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 54 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What one would want to do is compare the text of Amendment LXVIII, clause 1, as translated here with the translation in the Badinter Commission report which is no longer in front of me. It is just the top of page 4, I believe. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could Prosecution Exhibit 52 be returned to Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Badinter cites Constitution, presumably, LXVIII, that, "The citizens exercise their powers through a representative Assembly or by referendum". Actually, LXVIII does say, and you will see the translation here, that is not quite correct, that "Citizens are the bearers of power, which they exercise through representatives in assemblies of social-political communities, by referendum", and that is where Badinter stopped, "in public meetings and other forms of personal declaration of opinion".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Based upon Amendment LXVIII, instead of LXVII, would you, Professor Hayden, share the conclusion of the Badinter Committee that the plebiscite of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina was outside the framework of the Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would be much more hesitant than Mr. Badinter apparently was, because it seems to me that a plebiscite is a form of personal declaration of opinion, and this is clearly provided for in the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, the Badinter Committee suggested that possibly a referendum could clarify the existing uncertainty, as you have told us. Was a referendum then held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A referendum was, indeed, held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the decision was taken that a referendum would be held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The referendum -- the decision to hold this referendum was taken in a session of the Bosnian Parliament, or purports to have been taken in a session of the Bosnian Parliament, on 24th 28 and 25th January 1992, which was another quite dramatic occasion in the short life of the Bosnian Parliament that had been elected in the free and fair elections of 1990. The decision to take a referendum, to have a referendum, was proposed by the SDA, the Muslim Party, with some support from HDZ politicians, but it was primarily an SDA sponsored action. It was opposed by the SDS, by the Serbian representatives. Now, again this was a very long session, a very, shall we say, lively session, of the Bosnian Parliament that again went to one of these sessions that went until very late at night or actually early in the morning, and there was clearly a great deal of negotiation. The Serb representatives were in the Parliament. They had come back into the Parliament that they had, essentially, walked out of in October, and were involved in attempting to negotiate a compromise on this position. In fact, at a late stage in these parliamentary proceedings, Mr. Karadzic, who was head of the SDS, and the Vice President of the SDA, took the podium together to announce that they had reached a deal, that the internal structures of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be reorganised and then immediately, or actually 30 days thereafter, there would be a referendum.
