According to the newspaper accounts of the main Sarajevo paper, Oslobodjenje, and the independent Serbian paper, Borba, and the independent Serbian weekly, Vreme, this announcement was greeted with a great deal of applause. However, after a pause in the parliamentary session, 28 Mr. Izetbegovic returned to the podium and said that there could not be any preconditions for a referendum, that a referendum would have to take place. The leader of the Serbian caucus, in the SDS caucus, in the Parliament, demanded that the question be referred to the Committee on the establishment of equality of the nations and nationalities. This was a session that had now gone until about 3.30 in the morning. The speaker of the parliament, still Mr. Krajisnik of the SDS, proclaimed an end to the day's session and said that the Parliament would meet again -- this is 3.30 in the morning -- he says the Parliament will meet again at, I believe, 10.30 the same morning, in other words, seven hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What would then happen, Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what then happened was that after an hour the -- again a Muslim member of the Parliament proclaimed the Parliament to be in session, and Muslim and Croat Members of the Parliament passed an Act to hold the referendum by a vote of something like 134 and obviously none against, since there was no one else in the room, again below the two-thirds of 160. They did actually a little bit of other business then by themselves and then they left. When the Speaker of the Parliament showed up when he called the session at 10.30 in the morning, he walked in with the members of the SDS, waited an hour, determined that they had no quorum and ended the session. So, I believe, ends the active life of the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the 28 composition in which it was elected in the free and fair elections of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What, Professor Hayden -- it is a similar question as I did put to you before -- what was the authority of this SDA member in Parliament to decide that the Assembly would gather, not at 10 o'clock that morning in order to decide on the referendum, but to do it one hour later, one hour after 3.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea what authority he would have cited, if indeed he cited an authority, it is possible he did. Of course, recalling that Mr. Krajisnik was Speaker of the Parliament as part of the same overall package that had made Mr. Izetbegovic President of the presidency and Mr. Pelivan President of the government, any authority that he claimed would probably be seen as a rejection of the entire deal that had structured the coalition government in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, what is your opinion about a constitutionality of this outvoting of the Serbian members of the Bosnian and Herzegovinan Parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would seem, on the face of it, to be contrary to the valid Amendment LXX, clause 10, of the then valid Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, this was the decision-making to hold the referendum. What was the result of the referendum that was finally held, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The referendum that was actually held on February 29th and March 1st of 1992 was even more of an ethnic census, a national census, nationality census, than the elections of 1990 had been. Approximately -- Professor Gow has discussed this as well 28 -- 65 per cent or so of the electorate voted. Virtually no Serbs voted, virtually everyone who voted "yes". So you have a rather curious referendum in which there is no opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if we just stay apart from the legitimacy of this referendum, could the outcome of the referendum be regarded to reflect the will of the peoples -- I use the plural as well -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is well put. The Badinter Commission had said that the will of the peoples had not been established, the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to an independent state had not been established, and that this might possibly be established by a referendum. I do not think that you could possibly interpret the results of this referendum as having established the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constituting the Republic as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So, Professor Hayden, saying that this referendum did not reflect the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute the Republic, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a sovereign independent state, could you please tell us whether the Badinter Committee in the opinions 4, 8 and 11 was consistent in its opinion as far as the criteria for the existence of an independent state were concerned? Perhaps I should give you the opportunity to look at the Badinter opinions 4, 8 and 11. 4 is Exhibit Prosecution Exhibit 53, if I am correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: And 8 is Prosecution Exhibit 54 -- no, 4 is 52, 8 maybe Exhibit 28 53 and 11 maybe Prosecution Exhibit 54. So 52, 53, 54.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 52 I have, so it is 53 and 54. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: While you are looking at that, Professor Hayden, why, in your opinion, did the February 29 referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina not represent the will of the people when 65 per cent of the electorate voted but virtually no Serbs? Secondly, do you know whether there is any evidence that Serbian people were encouraged not to vote in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to the first question, the question, the failing that Badinter perceived at the time of the opinion 4 was clearly the will of the peoples, plural, and he was distinguishing between the Serbs and between the Croats and the Muslims. In doing so, he was following Bosnia and Herzegovina constitutional structures and Bosnia and Herzegovina political practice. It was very clear at that moment that the will of the peoples, plural, had not been established. The referendum, I believe Dr. Gow mentioned as well, that very few Serbs voted in the referendum, and it is fairly clear that most of them did not want to vote in the referendum. They had themselves had a plebiscite in November that had been referred to by Badinter and had voted virtually 100 per cent to remain within Yugoslavia. Now, in Yugoslavia from 1990, 1989/1990 onwards, we have also its referenda, and they are always taken by close to 100 per cent of the vote in favour of the Party that organised them, and we have a Serbian one like this, and then we have a Croat/Muslim one like this. Certainly, Serbs were not encouraged by Serbian Parties to vote in the referendum of 28 February 29th and March 1st, as they had been encouraged to vote in the plebiscite. It is, however, very doubtful that many Serbs would have voluntarily voted in this referendum which, as I say, was essentially an ethnic census. In that sense, you see, the results of the referendum were absolutely congruent with the situation that was clearly there on the ground at the time that Badinter No. 4 was written, which was that the Serbs had expressed themselves very clearly against constituting Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state and Croats or Muslims, particularly, and then Croats a little more nuanced were for it. In that regard, you see, the referendum taught no one anything that they did not already know, which was that some of the peoples, the Bosnian constitutional and politically recognised peoples, were in favour of independence and some were not. Since Badinter had stated that this was the question, I think it would be impossible to interpret the results of the referendum as providing a positive answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So it did not represent the will of the people because ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Peoples, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- peoples, oh, yes, that is very important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the question, it is the peoples, and that was how it was expressed by Badinter and that was in keeping with Bosnian constitutional structure and political practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It did not represent the will of the peoples because a group of 28 the peoples, i.e. the Serbs, boycotted the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would put it as one of the peoples, one of the peoples. One of the peoples was against and two of the peoples, narods again, narodi, are for, which Badinter had noted in his opinion and it is suggested that this could possibly, possibly, have been resolved by a referendum. If, in fact, a referendum had been held and everyone had voted, perhaps one could have interpreted it that way which was probably what Badinter had in mind, which was probably as well why the Serbs boycotted it, to make their vote in the referendum, as it were, absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But I am afraid I do not understand what Badinter is talking about. It seemed to be perfectly clear that the wills of the peoples were disparate; that one of the peoples wanted one thing, the other two wanted something else. How could you possibly get the will of the peoples, plural?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Badinter in opinion 4 was actually hesitant about this, and said that this could possibly be shown by a referendum -- could possibly be shown -- but the ways in which the referendum was held and the voting patterns in it indicate to me that this was not shown; that all the referendum did was confirm exactly what you point out, your Honour, that one of the peoples was for this and two of the peoples were against this. Of course, this is your bind in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that you have no single majority narod that could impose its will on the others, but that you had to work by consensus. The consensus had clearly broken down and the constitutional structures that were designed 28 to foster consensus had also broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, is this reference to the constitutional structure a reference to the prohibition to outvote other peoples? Is this a reference to the right of secession for the peoples, each of it, each of the constituent parties, in that Republic? Is that what you say, that what Badinter proposed finally turned out to be unconstitutional -- at least suggested, I should not, when I listen well to you, he did not propose a referendum but he suggested that possibly that might be of some help and it finally turned out to be unconstitutional as it was held.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to ponder the constitutionality of it in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Certainly, the way it was scheduled in regard to Badinter's suggestion seems to have been brought about unconstitutionally. To schedule this referendum that Badinter had suggested was not done in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the parliamentary manoeuvring sounds extremely dubious as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I will come back to the consistency of Badinter in his opinions 4, 8 and 11 that have been presented to you. Could you explain whether there are any inconsistencies in these subsequent opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Opinion No. 4 -- I am sorry, opinion No. 8 ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you refer to specific parts, I would like you to put it on the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would have to find them to do this. It is dated July 4th of 1992. Right, clause 3 -- I do not have it on my monitor. I 28 do not know if you have it on yours. There we are. Yes, OK. The referendum proposed in opinion No. 4 was held -- proposed, yes, OK -- on 29th February/1 March a large majority of the population voted in favour of the Republics independence. This is a statement of July 4th. That is opinion No. 8. As for No. 11 -- I am sorry, I have to find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think 11 was 54.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is paragraph 6. OK. "In opinion No. 4 issued on 11 January, the Arbitration Commission came to the view that 'the will of the peoples ... could not be held to have been fully established'. Since then, in a referendum held ... the majority of the people have expressed themselves in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia". I find that a significant difference in wording, "the majority of the people", as opposed to "the will of the peoples".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could this difference in wording perhaps be explained by the situation that existed at the time the opinion No. 11 was delivered compared, for example, to the time when opinion 4 was delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would suggest that that is probably so. Opinion 4 was written in January of 1992 and the question was whether recognition should be granted. Opinion 8 was written in January -- in July. 11, also after that. Recognition had been granted in April, so that recognition was a fait accompli. Badinter was then confronted with a situation in which, if he were to maintain his original criterion, the political decision to recognise would have been mistaken, and I do not wish to impute 28 anything to Mr. Badinter but I do find the circumstances to be significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, in your opinion and applying the Badinter definition of a state as a community which consists of a territory and a population subject to an organised political authority, was by late 1991 Bosnia and Herzegovina empirically a state or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By those criteria, certainly by early 1992 on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were three communities, not one, there was no single community. Organised political authority, as defined by the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had clearly broken down. Thus I would say that by the Badinter criteria Bosnia was not empirically a state after that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, your testimony seems to indicate that the processes that took place throughout the former Yugoslavia and brought about this dissolution, also took place within Bosnia-Herzegovina and led similarly to the dissolution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you perhaps point out the main points whether this really is what your statement is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is the essence of my statement and I might simply provide a summation. Yugoslavia was created was created after World War I and the basic premise of Yugoslavia was that the South Slavic peoples were so closely related to each other that they could co-existed, so intermingled that they had to co-exist. Empirically both of these were true. However, that is not what won in the free and fair elections of 1990. What succeeded state socialism in Yugoslavia in 1990 was the separate 28 nationalisms of the Yugoslav peoples, the narodi, nationalisms by which each people would get its own state; the narod, the ethnic group in American terms, gets the state, the territory and the government. This is what won in 1990, this is what people voted for. Voting for this, this construction is possible if not exactly admirable as I think Judge McDonald suggested yesterday in a question to me. In most of the Yugoslav Republics the problem is in Bosnia and Herzegovina where there was no majority narod in whom sovereignty could reside. Bosnia and Herzegovina could have existed as a state under this political definition if the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina chose to view themselves as Bosnians. I think quite tragically in the free and fair elections in 1990 they did not. They partitioned themselves into Serbs, Croats, Muslims and others which, of course, the possibility was always there, the presence of these groups was always there. Groups with strikingly, peoples in Yugoslav terms, narods, with strikingly different views of what the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be, with some of them certainly the dominant Serbian political opinion, and quickly the dominant Croatian political opinion in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that, as the Yugoslav Constitutions had said, it was the narod that had the right to self-determination and that they had the right, as Slovenia and Croatian had seceded from Yugoslavia, to secede from Bosnia and Herzegovina and did not want to be included in this state. The constitutional and political structures devised 28 to prevent this type of breakdown in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did not function and the constitutional order of the state dissolved, leaving these three communities. I find this a situation in which civil war was absolutely inevitable for one of two reasons. If Bosnia were to be constituted as a state empirically within its borders in the former Yugoslavia, it would have been opposed militarily on those peoples who rejected it, or alternatively they had made it, both the Serbs and the Croats, quite clear that they would fight to avoid being included in the state that they rejected, and that is indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour. I have a just technical issue, but first if you want to put any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, it was just one question really. I suppose it relates to history and you have said you are not a historian. You have taken us from World War I, at the close of World War I, when this state of Yugoslavia was created and then you take us to free elections. Well, you talked a little bit before that, 1989 the amendments to the Constitution in Slovenia, then Croatia and then of course in 1990, in 1991 we get to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell us what was the role of Tito or the effect that Tito's reign, so to speak, during that interim period after World War II, and how perhaps Tito either as an individual or the way that the Constitutions were structured was able to hold these divergent narods together? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the basic principles of Tito's Yugoslavia, as I think I said when I read those extracts from the Slovenian intellectuals, one of the basic principles was brotherhood and unity, bratstvo-jedinstvo, that Slovenian intellectuals at the time, by the late 80s, were rejecting, brotherhood as terror and unity as homogenization and they rejected this. Tito and the partisans were very aware of what the consequences of a breakdown of Yugoslavia would be. World War II in Yugoslavia had been, among other things, a quite ghastly civil war which in terms of numbers of victims, absolute numbers of victims on a smaller population base, was much worse than what we have seen in Yugoslavia since 1991. Tito and the partisans having thought that, and this was part of it, it was a war against occupiers but there were some ghastly civil wars and what they interpreted as a communist revolution all going on simultaneously. I would say that we have not seen anything in Bosnia since 1991 that we did not see in Bosnia between 1941 and 1945. Tito and company were aware of this and this is why they set up a federal state. Their idea was to give maximum autonomy to these nations so that none would feel constrained. What happened was that from the first Constitution of 1945 until the last Constitution in 1974, and there was also effectively a new Constitution in '54, there was one in '63, the constitutional structures became so loose that it became a de facto confederation which then Slovenia and Croatia used to bring down the entire structure. I might address it in another way. The problems of 28 Bosnia and Herzegovina were certainly not new to the 1990s. As I said, you a had civil war in the 1940s. People in Bosnia, if I can use Bosnians, Bosanci as opposed to Bosnjaci, had lived together for many centuries, but the centuries have been punctuated by periods of violence and these have tended to occur after the larger state that has encompassed Bosnia-Herzegovina has collapsed or a state authority has been withdrawn. There were periods when Bosnia was part of the Ottoman empire until 1878. When the Ottoman empire withdrew there was a great deal of violence and many Muslims left for Turkey with the Otomans. When Austro-Hungarian empire collapsed at then end of World War I there was a great deal of ethnic violence. When the first Yugoslavia collapsed in 1941 there was a great deal of ethnic violence, and when the second Yugoslavia collapsed in 1991/1992 the division of the population was something that had certainly occurred before and the results were something that had certainly occurred before. There is a curious sense in which it was the fear of all this that, in effect, forced the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina to partition themselves looking for safety in the numbers of their fellow narod and, thus, bringing about the destruction of the common state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So that really it was the force or was it the force of Tito's personality that was able to hold the republics together, even though by their Constitutions they were given significant or a modicum, I do not know whether it is significant, but some independence and freedom, but the force of his personality permitted the republics to stay together, is that so or not 28 so ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a sense ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- or is that an overstatement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. What permitted the republics to stay together was the overarching structure of the communist party of Yugoslavia, because you might have viewed the separate republics as being almost administrative in character because political decisions were made by the communist party of Yugoslavia. Tito could hold this together. A part of the story of the disintegration of communist Yugoslavia was also the disintegration of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia into the Leagues of Communists of each of the separate republics. This does not sound unfamiliar. In the United States there is democratic party in California and there is a Democratic party in New York and then there is a democratic party of the United States of America, but this structure was then seized by the Republican leaderships to destroy the overarching federal party. At the same time that the Slovenes were proclaiming the supremacy of the Republican Constitution to the Federal Constitution, they were also proclaiming the supremacy of the Republican party organisations to those of the federal party. Tito certainly did not permit this to happen. Something similar was on the verge of happening in 1971 and Tito, largely through his personal authority, crushed it. The structures that Tito left behind to deal with the potential divisions of Yugoslavia, certainly were not adequate to the task. 28 I can also say that throughout the 80s, which was where I started my testimony, there were people in Yugoslavia, very thoughtful people, who were aware of the inadequacies of the Tito structures, beginning with economics of course but then going through the political structures, and wished to revise them but they were defeated by the separate national elites in the separate republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You said in 1910 that there were elections that really were divided according to ethnic lines. Is that not so? So, as early as then people were voting according to narods, their narods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the choice was given to vote more or less freely, then that is what they chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Under Tito, under communism, that was kind of just swept under a rug or at least contained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, elections were hardly free or fair in Tito's Yugoslavia. When I first went there in the early 80s one of the jokes people told me was that, "We don't have elections, we do have voting."

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So when that then disappeared and the former Yugoslavia had its first try at democracy in how many years would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, actually the last elections had been in the 1920s because of a dictatorship declared in 1929, so it was a long time. It was virtually 60 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So when they had their first chance at democracy they reverted back to their ethnic differences, and superimposed really their parties on these ethnic groups or on their ethnic groups, I suppose, is that not so? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The parties that won were the ones were the parties were ethnic parties. This is what won. Not all parties were ethnic parties. As I said, in Bosnia particularly there was a party headed by the Federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, a Croat from Bosnia, who was trying desperately to hold Yugoslavia together because he knew, as I can assure you everyone knew, what the consequences would be. This was a non-ethnic party. It was the League of the Reformists of Yugoslavia. It stood for a civil society, a state of equal citizens. As I said, it got about 6 per cent of the vote. That probably happened because that election was in November and in the elections in Croatia in May the Croatian Democratic Union had already won, had already made perfectly clear its intention of seceding from Yugoslavia. The Croatian Democratic Union that was active in Bosnia and Herzegovina was and is controlled by the Croatian Democratic Union in Zagreb. So that it already seemed as if the electorate in Bosnia would fracture, that the chances of saving Yugoslavia were non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So the conflict then was caused by what would you say, the clashing claims for nationalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the formulation accepted -- and that is not just Yugoslavia but more or less throughout central Europe -- that the state, the territory and the government, belongs to the one nation. As I say, the problem with Bosnia was that it did not have one nation in the Yugoslav sense. It had three. Remember that it was the nations of Yugoslavia that had united. It was the nations of Yugoslavia that had the right to self-determination 28 according to the Constitution and to the way that Yugoslavs thought about these things and the way that their political parties were operating. This meant that if the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina turned itself into peoples instead of a people, that it would be very difficult to envision how Bosnia and Herzegovina could remain, because overwhelmingly the political desire of the Croats of Herzegovina, if not the Croats of Bosnia and there was a division there, was to become part of Croatia. They were adjacent to Croatia. They felt themselves to be part of Croatia. This has in fact happened. De facto western Herzegovina is incorporated into the economic, political, communications systems of Croatia. It is de facto Croatia. This was clear that this was going to happen and it was also clear that the Serbs were losing interest in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. In this type of structure being a member of a minority, it is not simply a political minority. Our concepts of democracy are based on the principle that the majority and the minority can change. This is not the principle on which these states are based. The principle on which these states are based is that there is a permanent minority, and part of the function of the state is to ensure the superiority, the sovereignty of the majority. So that to be a member of a minority in one of these states is to be outside of the body sovereign, really in a sense outside of the body politic. This was what won and everyone knew this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Each narod had a majority in one of the republics except the 28 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So each Republic was free to express the sovereignty of its people, of its narods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of the narods with giving superiority to the majority narod in Croatia, in Slovenia, in Serbia, but not in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they had 36 per cent I guess -- was it 36 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims by 1991 were approximately 44 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You are absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So everyone was kind of going their separate way, and there were the narod, the Muslim narod in between with really no Republic to claim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only Republic they could claim would be Bosnia and Herzegovina in which they do not form a majority. For this reason there is very good evidence that the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the late 1980s was strongly in favour of the continuation of Yugoslavia, because they could see what would happen if Yugoslavia would disintegrate. There is good public survey data on this. In fact, the law on political organisations of Bosnia and Herzegovina prohibited the formation of political parties on an ethnic or national religious basis, in other words, a political party for a particular narod. There was very strong political support for this law in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990, but it was clear after the Croatian elections in Croatia in 1990 the success of HDZ in Croatia and the success of the HDZ among Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina 28 that, you know, this picture was not going to work, that the Croats were out, and the Serbs were as well, the Serbs and the Croats actually had a very similar picture of Bosnia and Herzegovina at this stage and they did not consider themselves to be part of it. The Muslims actually took the same position in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Serbs took in regard to Yugoslavia. The Serbs, as a Slovenian politician said yesterday, in the excerpt that I read yesterday, he said the downfall of Yugoslavia would be a catastrophe for the Serbs and they knew it, and the downfall of Bosnia would be a catastrophe for the Muslims and they knew that. But it would also be a catastrophe for everyone in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We are still trying to sort things out I suppose. With the secession of Croatia, with the secession of Slovenia, what Bosnia Herzegovina was left with was to stay in the federation with Serbia. The Muslim narod was already a minority and if they stayed in with the Serbian and Montenegrin they would be a significant minority, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, and yet if they were to secede, then the other groups could each feel themselves to be threatened as being in the position of a minority. This was divined. You are quite correct in starting it with the secession of Slovenia because within the former Yugoslavia there was no majority narod. The Serbs, like the Muslims in Bosnia, were about 45 per cent, maybe even lower, overall because you had all of these other people. The next largest group were the Croats, you have Muslims, Slovenes, Muslims, Montenegrins, Macedonians. The others, and 28 Albanians actually, not one of the narodi, the narods of Yugoslavia but 2 million Albanians in Serbia itself, so that there was no majority. There was a whole set of institutional structures that, well, we designed to promote consensus. As I said, they were supposed to provide maximum autonomy and to operate on consensus and they broke down, as similar mechanisms broke down in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so the ones in Bosnia and Herzegovina were patterned after federal ones. Slovenia's secession, you see, upset the demographic balance because there are suddenly 2 million less non-Serbs which would then increase, it increases the percentage of every population left, but it would increase the percentage of Serbs to the point where they would start to be close to being a majority nation which the others might then fear. Of course it certainly upset all of the political and constitutional structures of Federal Yugoslavia, just as those Bosnia later required participation and consensus, for this reason that in 1989 when I saw the Slovenian amendments I was very worried because it was clear that if Slovenia could reject the competence of the federation then other republics could as well, Slovenia's rejection of the only political mechanism left, the only political mechanism for resolving disputes between republics, left nothing other than the unilateral actions of the republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: There were two questions I would like to ask you, Professor. The first one is we have heard a great deal from individual witnesses about contentedly living together of 28 different ethnic groups, to the extent to which “my best friend is a Serb” or “I am godfather to a Croat”. Contrasted with that is the fact that we find that in villages in the opstina Prijedor they seem to be very clearly designated and understood by everyone as being Muslim villages or Serbian villages or Croat villages. How do you, if you do, reconcile those two views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In two ways. The greatest interminglings of populations in the former Yugoslavia were in cities and in the province of Vojvodina in Serbia, and in parts of Croatia that actually boarded Bosnia and Herzegovina areas called Banija and Slavonia. I suppose I could point to them on a map if you wished. In rural Bosnia and in some other rural parts of the country the traditional pattern had been that you would have Serb villages, Muslim villages, Croats villages, whatever, and there was much less intermingling and yet as the 1980s progressed, I mean as Yugoslavia became more prosperous, you know, people had cars, people would go from villages, they would go to Prijedor, they would go to Banja Luka, they would go to Sarajevo, went to university. They did mingle and this form of identity was not a primary form of identity to most people in the 1980s. I can also tell you that the nationalist movements did not arise in the regions, the republics or the regions within republics that were most mixed. They arose in the regions that were most homogenous. Slovenia, for example, or in Croatia the heartland of the HDZ was not in the mixed regions of Banija and Slavonia, but was in the regions that were almost purely Croat. 28 Similarly, the Serbian Party in Croatia, the SDS, was based in the part of Croatia, in Knin, that was and had been for centuries virtually entirely Serb. Nationalists in those homogenous areas more or less drove the politics, and to the detriment of the people living together, living intermingled, who in one sense could not believe that these things could happen but on the other sense could believe that these things could happen. If I may give an example, in the Croatian elections in 1990 the people in the mixed regions were Serbs and Croats were living together and intermarrying did not vote overwhelmingly for the nationalist parties. They voted for the Reformed Communists as a way to avoid this, but their communities were torn apart. The war in Croatia took place in the mixed areas and the mixture, you see, was no longer politically imaginable. As nationalism was, in a sense, brought to the mixed regions, and quite often physically brought to the mixed regions, that you might find that there would be violence committed against people in one place, not by the people from that place, at least not initially, but by people from outside, which can then start sparks of conflict within the people who had been living together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The other question I wanted to ask you was, you have spoken not at all about Greater Serbia and Greater Croatia. To the extent to which Serbs and Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina were tending towards separation from the other ethnic groups in Bosnia, was that something that was part of the ambitions of Croatia and of 28 Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly there were (and are) people in the elites, the ruling elites and the ruling parties of Croatia now, and I think Serbia perhaps at an earlier stage, who did indeed have this model. My difficulty had been that the matter as I had seen it discussed and presented by Dr. Gow was that it ignored the political activities of the people in Bosnia themselves who did, indeed, exercise a political will in 1990 and did, indeed, vote and act in ways that could only bring on a civil war, no matter what was going on really from outside. Bosnia has existed as part of a single larger state, but it is very hard for it to exist as an independent state on its own because then the question is, whose state is it? I do not know if I have answered your question satisfactorily; if I have not, I will try again, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say it could only but bring on civil war. I hope this is not a lesson that democracy does not work, because it seems to me that there are other ways to deal with an election that may place you in the minority in a country than to engage in violence. I mean, in the United States, we have often elections where people will say: "I am not going to vote because there is really no alternative. I am just going to boycott this election". If they choose to boycott it, then they get what they get, which is not much because you do not vote. If the election turns out in such a way that they are then a minority, it seems to me there should be a better answer than 28 civil war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you, your Honour, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know that it was inevitable. There should be other ways to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I try to put it in another way? I do not think it came out in the recitation of my curriculum vitae, but I actually started my professional career as a scholar of India.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: As a scholar in what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of India.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, India.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I thought you said "media"; if so ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, heaven forbid!

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- that would open up a whole other line of questions before we recess for lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that, I am a consumer, but I did substantial research in India and in many ways, you see, when I got to Yugoslavia after 10 years of dealing with India, Yugoslavia seemed easy. I mean, there are 29 states in India and there were only six republics in Yugoslavia. There were only two scripts in Yugoslavia. There are 14 in India, religions, languages, etc. India is the largest democracy in the world, and I have seen it function, and no democracy is perfect and neither is India's. It functions because the presupposition of India, and consciously constructed by the people who brought India to independence, was the principle that we are all Indians. A similar principle was used to justify Yugoslavia. 28 Actually, similar formlations were used. Nehru said there was an India because there was an Indian people because all of the various peoples of India were more alike each other than they were to anyone else on earth. A similar logic was used to justify the creation of Yugoslavia. As I said, the presupposition of Yugoslavia was that these peoples were so similar that they could coexist and so intermingled they had to. That did not succeed. What succeeded, this nationalism was also based on the premise that these people cannot, in fact, coexist, and when that succeeded in regard to the breaking up of the former Yugoslavia, the logic of the equation is, if there cannot be a common state of Serbs, Croats and others called Yugoslavia, how then can there be a common state of Serbs, Croats and others called Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the Serbs and Croats between them did outnumber the Muslims? So, I am not saying that democracy does not work in any sense. I am saying that in the situation that was produced by this very brief stab at democracy at the end of communism in 1990, the political constructions that won on all sides led to a situation where a civil war was inevitable in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not offer formally all the Exhibits that I have tendered today as evidence. I would like to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did you not? Let us identify them by number. Are you saying if you did not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I did not -- no. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Let us check over the lunch recess. Then I will ask if there is any objection and then we will admit them without objection. I think they are all in but we will see. We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, have you checked for your Exhibits that you offered?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was a mere form of question. I was told by those who are more familiar with Anglo American systems that I should tender the documents and then offer them as evidence. The only thing I wanted to do is to say they were offered as evidence. I think there is no misunderstanding as to the Exhibits tendered and now and then offered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are flexible. If I say that they are admitted, that means whatever, either they were offered, tendered, but they are in. I want to make sure that all of them have been admitted, and I guess they have, have they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. Cross-examination, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, you said in your evidence that you had spent quite a lot of time in Yugoslavia; indeed, I think you said you lived in Yugoslavia for a period of time. Is there any one 28 particular Republic that you spent most of your time in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spent most of my time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you also said in your introductory part that for a period of time -- I am sorry, I withdraw that -- you actually worked for Milan Panic in the London conference; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My five day diplomatic career!

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. Mr. Panic was then Prime Minister of the Federal Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the relationship is between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Slobodan Milosevic in a de facto sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in a constitutional sense, there is no relationship because Mr. Milosevic is President of Serbia which is one of the components of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is Mr. Zoran Lilic. In a de facto sense, it gets more difficult to answer, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic has certainly been involved in diplomatic negotiations, such as the Dayton peace negotiations over Bosnia in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am not sure in what capacity. I would imagine he was there in his capacity as President of Serbia, but he was certainly involved in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is true to say, is it not, that the FRY is, in a sense, a vehicle for Slobodan Milosevic? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many who would say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You would say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I might have to ponder it. I mean, certainly it is a much more complex situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you ever said it yourself, though, in any of your writings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I might have. I have written a lot in the last six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But I am asking you now whether you would agree with that as a proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly Mr. Milosevic is very central to the operations of Serbia and the SFRY, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I quote from an article which I believe you wrote called "The Constitutional Nationalism in the former Yugoslav Republics" ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Slavic Review 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I think on page 660 of that you say in the last paragraph: "The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1992, like the 1990 Serbian Constitution, must be viewed primarily as a vehicle for maintaining the personal power of Slobodan Milosevic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it in that way. I think the reason for that is that the constitutional power of the federation is low under the 1990 Constitution, and that the Presidents of the Republics, including Mr. Milosevic, of course, are involved in some of the federal institutions, such as the federal Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, would you see your main field as being that of a 28 constitutional lawyer or that of an anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this may surprise you actually, but I combined the two. Perhaps I should explain why I do so. As Yugoslavia entered its period of crisis which, as I said, began as economic and then became political and then became constitutional, there were a number of proposals for constitutional revisions, and notably from Slovenia and Croatia. When I analysed them, it became clear to me when I did a legal constitutional analysis of them they were proposals that were designed to ensure that there would be no workable state. Now, to a lawyer, of course, the purpose of a Constitution is to set up a workable state and then to put some control upon it. These proposals were, clearly, designed to ensure that there would be no workable state. Now, I found that to be very interesting. To explain it, I then had to go to my identity as an anthropologist and look into the cultural and social and political concepts that were driving this entire system, particularly this concept of narod, of nation, which is different from that normally used by Americans particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you spoke of that in your evidence, you also made reference in those constitutional provisions that you took us to -- you took us to numerous of them -- there was a broad definition, there was the definition of Serbia in the Serbian context or Croatia in the Croatian context, and then went on and said nations, nationalities; is it not possible that the definition intends to encompass all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think it is very clear, particularly in the context in 28 which these are presented, the political context, that the sovereign is the majority nation, ethnically defined. That is whose state it is. That is how I am looking at sovereignty. I suppose I was looking at it that way in part because I was used to socialist constitutions and then socialist constitutions clearly, the state is there not for the benefit of the entire population, but for only part of the population which is the working class, the working people. Conceptually, the structures of the post socialist constitutions are very, very similar. They also both contain the various rhetoric on, you know, human rights and freedoms and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, would you not, that the working class would itself, at least in part, encompass the nationalities as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, quite. The working class is a category that would cross cut all of the nations of Yugoslavia. It is one of the reasons why, you know, theoretically, Marx put it forth that way in contradiction to Herder and Hegel and the Romantics. It is set up this way in the Yugoslav Constitutions as well, and they really are through 1974 the Constitutions are there to advance the interests of the working class. But I might say that when that category that could include everyone was knocked out of the constitutions with the fall of socialism, what was left of the dual forms of sovereignty was actually a set of categories that were divisive, that divided the population, and the category that could unite the population was then taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But if you looked at everyone in the concept of a national, 28 being a member of a nation, and those definitions which incorporated specifically and enumerated nations as well as all others, does that not encompass the lot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a question of priorities and ordering. I mean, one could turn it around: why was it so very important for the incoming Croatian government elected in May 1990 already in July of 1990 to have immediately passed an Amendment that put Serbs into the category of these others if they were all the same? It was clearly important to the Croatian nationalist government to do it. It was very clearly important to the Serbs that it had been done. If they viewed it all as somehow a matter of essentially alphabetical ordering or something, they would -- none of them would have acted that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: True it is that there may be a political motivation for doing this, but surely you must agree with me that the definitions themselves lend themselves to an interpretation which would purport to cover all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, if we could envision a situation in which the US Constitution were amended to read, you know, "We, the white protestant people and others of the United States", the very fact that the amendment would be undertaken would be meaningful, and that political fact would also be meaningful in interpreting the wording of the constitution and the clauses that followed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell us, Dr. Hayden, what was the significance of the terms narod, nationalism, nation, under the Communist Tito's Yugoslavia? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance, it is clear that the term is included because it is one of the forms of identity of the peoples of Yugoslavia. It is also clear the Yugoslav constitutional distinction that Professor Gow discussed (and I have also tried to discuss) between the constituent nations, constituent narods, the state forming nations (as Dr. Gow described them), and the nationalities of those who have a republic of their own or a state of their own people outside of Yugoslavia. It was otherwise not of such importance. As I said, these were socialist constitutions and the primary goal of the constitutions was for them to be socialist constitutions. You did have the equal protection clauses of the federal Constitution that I believe I pointed out. One of the ways that I interpret the Slovenian Amendments in 1989, 43(C), and the autochthonous minorities and the like, it was kind of breaking the rules that had governed Yugoslavia until then. I mean, yes, the narodi, the nations, were in the Constitution, but everybody was guaranteed the right to equality and it was more or less treated this way, and suddenly distinctions were being made which seemed threatening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, is it not true that both legally and politically in Tito's communist Yugoslavia nationalism as such was, in fact, quite brutally suppressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nationalism in the sense of the political claim that each of the nations should have its own state, this was certainly suppressed and it was suppressed at the time of, in 1971, for example, at the time of the so-called mass movement, Maspok, in 28 Croatia. It was suppressed in other ways as well. Open espousals of national identity could get one into trouble. If one sang certain songs from World War II, for example, that were interpreted as being the songs of the Serb nationalist or the Croat nationalist, this could get you -- this could, indeed, get you into trouble of various degrees of seriousness in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, in the light of that, it would be quite odd, would it not, to give preeminence to nationalities in the Constitutions themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They have to be included. There is actually a great deal of work being done on this in East European studies. Clearly, nationalism did not vanish in Eastern Europe and even within East European communist countries. One might look at Romanija, for example, where the Romanijan Communist Party was also quite frequently a Romanijan nationalist party in regard to the Hungarian minority. Within Yugoslavia, national identity was not meant to be primary, and yet there were reasons of practical politics why it had to be included in the Constitution. But, as I say, it was not primary. These were primarily socialist constitutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, the word "national" appears in the description of the Yugoslav Army, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Yugoslovenska Narodna Armija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is usually translated as "Yugoslav People's Army".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which peoples? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could see the peoples of Yugoslavia and you could sometimes find it in that context. However, when it is compared (as it usually is in the Constitutions) with nationalities, the peoples and narodi, narodnosti, if you want, the nations and nationalities and the working class and all working people, it is very clear what was meant. Of course, by the time you get to Bosnia, then it is specified, you see, and it says that the narodi, peoples of Bosnia -- and the constitutions are wonderful because then they keep mixing the order, the peoples of Bosnia, the Muslims Serbs and Croats, and in the next article it will be the peoples of narodi, nations, the Serbs, Muslims and Croats, and they keep mixing up the order, but in the ordinary context one knew what the meaning was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who carried sovereignty, as it were, under the federal Constitution of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the federal Constitution was -- we were looking at some of the formulations yesterday afternoon -- the people, the nations and nationalities, narodi, narodnosti, of Yugoslavia, the working class and all working people. This is the formulation that one finds. Frequently, they are the ones, they are the actors. I suppose I could go back into my copy and point out some of the articles that I pointed out yesterday, and then some of the ones that I did not point out yesterday because there are so many in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the federal Constitution is made up of a combination of the Republics, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. You have a combination of Republics, yes. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do they not go to make up the sovereignty of the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what is the federation there for? I mean, who does it serve? Who does Yugoslavia serve? It serves the peoples of Yugoslavia, the narodi, narodnosti. It serves the working class and all working people who are the ones who are empowered to act. In some places, they realised their rights through the socialist republics. In other places, they realised their rights and obligations through the federation. There is a great deal of formulations along these lines there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, it is fair to say, is it not, that there is good political motive to create an aura of ambiguity about this issue in terms of nationalities, who has sovereignty, all of the people, the working class -- I am talking about the communist era -- it suited the regime, did it not, to not be too specific about any of these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in so far as these were socialist Constitutions and what was really supposed to matter was this socialist self-management, which is what the 1974 Constitution is really all about, yes, these are secondary issues that need not be taken too seriously. I actually became convinced with the start of Slovenian amendment crisis in 1989 that there were provisions of that Constitution that nobody had read. In a practical sense, they were not particularly relevant when the important decisions were being taken by the Party and so much of the Constitution was administrative. I might say that when the Party collapsed and the country was left to rely on the constitutional structures, the 28 constitutional structures somehow seemed to be less than adequate to the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just finally dealing with the situation as it evolved in Slovenia and Croatia after the passing of Tito, the wordings of the Constitution were such that they still had this broad ambit, did they not, except they had the removal of the term "working class"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear -- "still had this broad" what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Still had the broad ambit of description.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, ambit. Well, which part of it? I mean, when you remove the "working class", as I have just said, you are left with ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am dealing specifically with the state forming peoples.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are left with the nations and nationalities which, as I say, is implicitly divisive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Stephen asked you a question concerning the ability of people to move from one nationality to another nationality. Although you made reference to a movement to Yugoslav, you intimated that it was somewhat difficult to move into any other nationality, was that correct? Have I summarised what you said correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we are sure that we are speaking about the same thing, as I interpreted Judge Stephen's question, it had to do with one's identity as, for example, a Muslim or a Serb or a Croat. If we are talking about that, I just want to clarify that you are not talking about moving, for example, from within one Republic to another Republic. Is that the thrust of your question or is it the identity? 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, it is the identity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the identity. Well, as I said, there are, as I said to Judge Stephen, there are certainly factors such as personal names that might make it difficult to do this. There might be other reasons of custom or address for which it might be difficult to do this. As a practical matter, it is hard to say how many people changed their enunciation of their identities. The Yugoslav censuses permitted this to be a matter of free choice, and there are various books written on what the patterns of self-identification were. But it did not usually take place, except involving, perhaps, people who were themselves involved in with a product of mixed marriages, in other words, if one of your parents is a Serb and another is a Croat, you could declare yourself (and people sometimes did) on one occasion as a Serb, on another occasion as a Croat, possibly as a Yugoslav. I do not know if I am getting at your question actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are getting there. Perhaps I might clarify it by asking another question. Is there not indeed a policy that was applied during World War II to, in fact, convert a third, in a Croatian sense, to Catholicism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, if you are talking about the policy, the enunciated policy of the Ustasha government of Croatia of 1941 to 1945, that is how it has been reported as the Serbian problem of Croatia would be resolved by killing a third, expelling a third and converting a third, converting a third to Catholicism, and there were forced conversions that took place. Now, one has to remember that the primary 28 distinguishing feature of Serbs and Croats is religion, and it is Orthodox Christians among the Serbs and Catholics among the Croats. That has not always been the most important characteristic, and there is a great deal of history on this that I do not, perhaps, need to go into. Certainly, the forced conversions were, in a sense, inconsistent, certainly inconsistent with the type of ideology enunciated at that exact same time by the Nazi Party in Germany because one would think that conversion would not work. However, in the minds of the Ustasha it would work. This is not unprecedented only in the Balkans or in this part of the world. At the time of the partition of India in 1947, there were forcible conversions of Hindus to Islam. It is harder to be converted to Hinduism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the consequence of that is, is it not, that presumably in the minds of some Croatians, maybe not all, it would be quite acceptable for people to present themselves as Catholics if they were converted from Serbs, for example, the Serbian Orthodox religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one could certainly present oneself as a Catholic, particularly if one is a believer in Catholic, yes. I mean, what happens to the people who were forcibly converted? I cannot honestly tell you what the answer to that is. Those who adopted Catholicism and practised Catholicism could certainly consider themselves to be Catholics, and one does occasionally run into people who identify, on the one hand, as Serbs and as Catholics, although those are almost antithetical 28 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to the position in Serbia at the period after Tito's death, did the Serbian Socialist Party and the League of Communists in Montenegro, effectively, transform themselves into nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was a significant fear, was there not, by the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina which arose as a consequence of -- I am talking about 1991 and onwards -- what had happened during the period of World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there certainly was. Part of the breakdown of Yugoslav socialism involved, well, in a sense, resurrecting the bodies that had been buried since 1945. As I said earlier this morning, we have not seen anything in Yugoslavia since 1991, you know, 1991 to 95, that we did not see from 41 to 45, and much of that, the specifics of that, had been suppressed and the various nationalist parties in Slovenia, in Croatia, in Bosnia, brought it back. People had not forgotten in fact. They had simply not pursued this. You had the uncovering of mass graves, for example, in Slovenia, in Croatia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is not that people did not know that they were there. I mean, it turns out if you got to that region people did know, but part of living together after 1945 was never to pretend that it had not taken place, never to pretend that. Everyone did know that it had taken place. It was part of the official historiography of Tito's Yugoslavia, that this had been a ghastly period, and hence brotherhood and unity was necessary. Yet, at the same 28 time the individual actions themselves were often unmemorialised and people were willing to live with this for quite a long time as part of living together and not dwelling upon what had happened in the old Yugoslavia or in 41 to 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This, though, was assisted, was it not, by a propaganda campaign entered into by the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among others, yes, indeed. The Slovenes, the Croats, the Slovenian government, the Croatian government, the Serbian government, were all engaged in publicising the uncovering, the recovery of these mass graves. They were turned into political occasions of enormous importance in Slovenia and in Croatia where the aim was to uncover the bodies of people who had been massacred by the partisans. Among Serbs in Croatia, certainly the uncovery, recovery, of mass graves and the like was publicised as it had been in Croatia and Slovenia, although these were Serbs who were put into the graves by, as the reporting was, by the Croats or the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was not just a question of publicising the point. It was, in fact, a propaganda campaign by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One of several, just as there were propaganda campaigns by the Slovenes and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But what was the nature of the propaganda campaign of the Slovenes and the Croats in relation to genocide or the killing of the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What the Slovenes and the Croats were doing in, I believe it was, the summer of 1990, and I have the volumes and I have the commemorative volumes in my library in Pittsburg, the volumes 28 that they put out, you know, with the pictures of the bodies and the like, and the point of it was to de-legitimate the communist rule of Yugoslavia. Part of the methodology of Yugoslavia, of course, had been the partisans were the good guys and evidence of partisan atrocities had been covered up. I can tell you that an actual census of victims of World War II was conducted in Yugoslavia in the early 1960s, although it was never published and, in fact, is literally impossible to get hold of. One of the problems of the people conducting it was they did not know what to do with the victims of the partisans. So, the Croats and the Slovenes were using these to throw into question the legitimacy of Yugoslavia. I just might say, I remember distinctly -- the implication was that "We cannot live together because we were involved in killing each other" -- I remember distinctly a political cartoon in the Croatian news weekly, Danas, when it was still independent, more or less, and it showed several men in, I believe, business suits in a room lined with skulls and bones and one saying to the other: "Is this really the appropriate place to discuss constitutional changes?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But was there not a revisionist propaganda campaign being carried out ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- in Croatia which is the opposite of what you are saying now, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there not a denial? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there not a denial being made by Croatia that these things did not happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry -- which things are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These mass killings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the new Croatian regime was publicising the killings of Croats that had taken place by the partisans. They are publicising this, as are the Slovenes. Now, this is revisionist. I mean, this is clearly revisionist in regard to the historiography to the time of Yugoslavia, which was that the partisans were the good guys and, I mean, they may have executed people in the name of the people, but that they had engaged in mass slaughter was not part of the accepted his historiography and was not openly written about within Yugoslavia. You could find it elsewhere, including some extraordinary descriptions in the book by Milovan Djilas, "Wartime", but that was published outside of Yugoslavia. So that was a revisionist campaign -- is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am directly referring to an article that you have written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gathered that, but I was not sure what your reference was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "Balancing Discussions of Jasenovac and the Manipulation of History", and on page 212 of that you say: "Part of this propaganda war centred on revisionist histories of massacres during and just after World War II, with Croat writers denying the genocidal activities of the NDH, and some Serb intellectuals giving wildly inflated figures of the dead".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK, I am sorry. I was referring to different figures. Part of 28 the accepted historiography of World War II was that the Ustasha, rulers of Croatia, the state that was -- the independent state of Croatia that existed at the time of the German control of Yugoslavia, that it had committed genocide against Serbs, and Serbs, Jews, gypsies and others of the usual formulations in Croatia. Now, whether this was so or not became an issue with Croatian historians saying that this really was not -- that this really did not happen. It tended to focus around the works of Dr. Tudjman who was now President of Croatia and who had published a book in 1989 called "Bespuca ... The Wastelands of Historical Reality". The main thrust of the book was that, well, you know, there were certainly killings there, but the numbers are wildly inflated and, by the way, the death camp at Jasenovac that Serbs complain about was actually being run by Jews and, you know, the things that happened there were happening to Croats. Now, while Dr. Tudjman is attempting to minimise the numbers killed, there are Serbian historians who are trying to maximise the numbers killed, and who are saying that a million Serbs were killed at Jasenovac alone which is ridiculous. I mean, it clearly is ridiculous. There were serious attempts to estimate the casualties in Yugoslavia during World War II and actually consist -- quite close figures were reached independently by a Serb author and by a Croat author in the mid 1980s and they were about 1 million, and they broke down reasonably comparably as well in terms of who was what. But, 28 what drove the discussion was the politics of, on the one hand, Croatian historians saying that, you know, this had all been overblown and, on the other hand, Serbs saying it had all been underplayed, and serious scholarly work tended to get lost in the cross-fire.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did you say that, I do not know how to pronounce it ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: J-A-N-E-S-O-V-A-C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Close. J-A-S-E-N-O-V-A-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was located in the Prijedor region, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was actually located across the river in Croatia, Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But north west, I guess?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would have to look at the map to know exactly where it is, but, yes, it is close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not too far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is reasonably close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that camp was run by Jews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that, no. I say that President Tudjman suggests that in a portion of the 1990 edition of his book which, I understand, has since been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that the thesis he wrote at the university or what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was a book that he wrote, that Dr. Tudjman is now in his 70s, this is a book that he wrote in the late 1980s. It is a very interesting read, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But, in any event, the wildly inflated figures given of 28 the number of dead primarily suited the Serbian interests who may have wanted to stir up nationalistic feelings among the population; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, just as the raising the number of -- in the first place bringing in the category of Croats killed by the partisans and then raising that as high as possible serves an interest of Croatian leaders at the time. Yes, I wrote a quite substantial article about all of this called "Recounting the Dead", which I do not know if you have, but I will send you one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. The type of constitutional nationalism that you spoke of in the 1990s, was it a similar type of Constitutional nationalism that operated in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it a similar type of constitutional nationalism that operated in Serbia as opposed to when compared to the other republics of Croatia and Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Constitutionally, it is harder to find in Serbia, although one certainly does find it in the preamble to the Serbian Constitution, which I cite in what we exhibited, the article that is supposedly on the streets now, and I believe I cited in the articles that you are looking at. Certainly, one found it most openly expressed in the Croatian Constitution. Serbia, however, Serbian politics seemed less tightly bound to constitutional norms than, perhaps, in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian political structure in many ways did not change overly from the socialist period. It is many of the same 28 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving on to Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, you say in an article that is entitled "Nationalism in former Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is entitled?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I apologise, "Constitutional Nationalism" ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- "in the former Yugoslav Republics". You say: "Until late 1992 Constitutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not reflect constitutional nationalism", what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my formulation of constitutional nationalism, which I have forgotten exactly the page number in there, but I do define it, it is a constitutional and legal structure that privileges one narod, nation, ethnically defined over others in the state. I say that you do not find this in Bosnia and Herzegovina because you do not have a single majority narod who can be in that privileged position. Instead, you have got the three narodi and then the nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that it was not possible to devise a constitutional structure that would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But why did you say until late 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. When did I actually publish that article? The date of is 1992. Did I stop then or did something happen that I am trying to remember five, four years later?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It appears to be published in the winter of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well, there is a little -- I am sure it came out in 1993 with a cover date of 1992. If that is what you are referring to, I would, presumably, have stopped there because that, you 28 know, is when I had to get it back to the publisher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. So you are not suggesting that there was some sort of change in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember -- certainly not for the Bosnian Constitution in 1992. I am not suggesting that. I think I am just stopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the same article, you go on to say: "While the leaders of the group agreed to share power at the level of the opstina, the victorious party of the majority ethnic group took absolute control over local government purging all not of their nation", this is referring specifically to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
