utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you saying this is a general thing or are you saying there are exceptions to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I imagine there probably are exceptions to it, but I was writing on the basis of the information available to me at the time. However, I might add that I believe it is the 1994 Country Reports of the US State Department on Bosnia-Herzegovina said that in the areas controlled by the SDA it is absolutely one Party rule, and in the areas controlled by the HDZ it is absolutely one Party rule, and thus monoethnic rule. The State Department thinks highly of those folks. I mean, those are friends. So I think it is a pattern that by the reports apparent to me in 1992, from sources that seemed credible to me, seemed true, and it certainly rings true with what has happened since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you would not be surprised to hear that there was, at least that we know of, one exception to that? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not be surprised at an exception, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the same article you speak of democracy being still birth especially and you say specifically in Serbia as a consequence of this nationalism. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The project I am working on now, as I said at the start of my testimony, is actually called "Potemkin Democracies, Serbia and Croatia since 1990", so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I raised with you earlier the question of propaganda and particularly propaganda in Serbia. It is true, is it not, that Milosevic in Serbia took a particular type control over media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milosevic in Serbia was the first to take particularly tight control over the media in a Yugoslav Republic, and it was a recipe that was followed by the HDZ government as soon as it took power. So, he was one of, yes, and certainly freedom of the media is not a characteristic that we associate with the region where people speak Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also spoke in your evidence of moves being taken by Slovenia in relation to, if I can express it this way, upsetting the constitutional arrangement by making amendments and so forth. Did Slovenia do that on its own, I think as you suggested first, or was it provoked into this by other events that happened in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday, what you have with the demise of state socialism in the former Yugoslavia, because I think this is one where I started yesterday, you have the question arising of what will replace state socialism, and you have the rise of nationalist movements as well as people attempting to promote a 28 type of liberal democracy that we would recognise in western Europe. So that these efforts are going on. I am afraid I have lost my train of thought. I am sorry. What was your question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am asking you whether the events in Slovenia ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, right. I am sorry. The Slovenes are, indeed, part of this. So the reason I was introducing the comments of the Slovenian intellectuals yesterday and recounting my own experiences in Slovenia in the late 1980s was that nationalism was certainly rising in Slovenia, and nationalism rising in Slovenia was rising at the same time as some people were speaking of it in Serbia, and this is before the arrival of Slobodan Milosevic; the discussions in the Exhibit, the pages from Dnevni Telegraf, the discussions that took place before Milosevic arrived on the scene. Milosevic certainly was the first to take power with a nationalist tinge to it, but followed by Slovenes. When we are talking about the constitutional processes, constitutionally it was clear to me in the summer of 1989 when I obtained the draft of the Slovenian Amendments that if these Amendments were valid, then Yugoslavia was invalid. This seemed to me to be extremely dangerous, because if the Yugoslav federation, the federal organs, were to cease to exist, there are no mechanisms then for resolving conflicts between republics and that is, indeed, what happened. I actually published (along with a colleague from the Belgrade Law School) an article setting out this scenario. It 28 was first thing I ever published in a Yugoslav newspaper. It was a short article in Borba in September of 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, with the proposition, that there was growing hostility between Serbia and Slovenia in 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This arose, among other things, out of what was happening in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there was increasing hostility between Serbia -- I am sorry Serbia and Slovenia throughout 1989, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this hostility between Serbia and Slovenia was instrumental in the passing of the Amendments to the Slovenian Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure it had a lot to do with it. It was part of the political climate at the time, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the word "instrumental"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure because it was a very important part of the political climate of Slovenia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had Slobodan Milosevic captured the Serbian media by 1987?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the end of '87, yes -- most of the Serbian media, the most important media, the most important daily papers and the television station, yes. It is curious that Serbia has until this day maintained a couple of independent media, but they are of limited circulation but superb quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Speaking of the elections in Serbia in 1990, were they seen as fair and free elections in the same way as they were seen as elections in the other parts of what was the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the phrase used by international observers was "free 28 but not fair" because of the control over the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, opposition rallies were not covered by the media and there are misquotes and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a result of that election, Slobodan Milosevic captured 194 of the 250 votes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his Party did, yes, the Socialist Party of Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The implementation of the process of ethnic cleansing that occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you agree with me that that impacted most severely and extensively upon the non-combatant civilian community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The non-combatant civilian community has certainly suffered the most in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have not concentrated on the processes of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what occurred there was aided by paramilitary groups, including those controlled by Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am now -- you are now asking questions that I am less confident on, but I believe those were the reports at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you see a parallel between what occurred in Nazi Germany in the period of 1930 up to 1940 and this process of what was occurring with nationalism, with the emergence of dominant ethnic groups in Yugoslavia in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what you mean by a "parallel" here. I find that nationalism of this type, associating nation, narod, ethnic group in American terms, with state, which is a territory and a government, to be a very central European formula. I do not read German. My colleagues who do tell me that this Germany 28 constitutional thought goes this way. Of course, you see this in the citizenship laws of Germany. What I have been looking at in my work, citizenship laws are part of it and discriminatory citizenship laws and certainly denaturalising, if you will, people who had been citizens of a state, as has happened to Jews in Germany in 1934, as happened to people in the post Yugoslav republics, and this is certainly part of it. It is all part of the image of who actually belongs in the state, whose state it is. I am not sure if that is what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Do you say that that has its foundations in these Constitutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say that these Constitutions put forth a vision of the state that is congruent with that image. It depends on how far it is then taken. Conceptually, those who are not of the majority nation do not really belong in the state. It is not theirs. I mean, that is why they are not part of the sovereign group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that part of the constitutional framework or is it more correct to say that it was part of the political philosophy of the nationalist parties at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually view it as a cultural logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may do, but is it reflected through the political process, is the point that I am raising, such as, for example the HDZ, the SDS or the SDA in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is certainly reflected in who wants to join these parties. It may also be reflected in what happens after the election. I have viewed some of the processes that have taken place after 28 these elections as being an inversion of what Americans call affirmative action, negative action, if you will. The point of the state is certainly not to ensure equality of an equal body of citizens. It is to ensure the superior status of the majority nation. This is where in very many ways that frequently people would lose rights, would lose employment, would lose ultimately the right to citizenship on an ethno-national basis. This is very logical if you come into this framework of thought. It is not a logic that I like, but it is a logic that I try to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But would you agree with me if I put to you that particularly, say, in Bosnia-Herzegovina this was directed more as a political philosophy, for example, of the SDS, rather than there being any specific constitutional measures in operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I see the SDS and the HDZ, particularly, as being very similar in these structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the sake of balance, I am happy to include the HDZ, but I am saying would you agree with me that this is a political ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a political logic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- logic, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is political logic, yes. It is a very strong political logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It certainly was not derived, was it, from the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, not from the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina 28 which was written and amended under state socialism, and no new Constitution was ever written for Bosnia and Herzegovina, unless we now count the Dayton Constitution, but that was not written by people from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It would not be under the Constitution of Serbia either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you can see the logic reflected in whose state it is in the preamble. The Serbian Constitution defines Serbia as a state of equal citizens in probably Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nor would it be Croatia in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I am saying is that the political structure which would see the bringing about of the domination and exclusion of the other non-ethnic group is not reflected in the Croatian Constitution in terms of what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure of the connection with Bosnia and Herzegovina. I interpret the Constitutions in part in the context of what the politicians are saying. It may not be expressed in the Croatian Constitution, but it is clearly expressed whose state it is. Mr. Tudjman has been very clear about whose state it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but not in relation specifically when dealing with the constitutional provisions of Croatia could that apply to the political activities of the Parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina is my point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in so far as the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina is controlled by the HDZ of Croatia, and it is, are we in a constitutional framework here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you saying that we are? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. I mean, supposedly we are not, and yet it was the HDZ in Zagreb that was able to change the leader of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina in early -- in late April/early May of 1992, replacing Mr. Kljuic with Mr. Boban, and the comment was that Mr. Kljuic had proved to be too much Bosnian and not enough Croatian. Is that within the constitutional structures? I would doubt it very much. Is that the political reality? Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is, essentially, what I am suggesting to you ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- that it is political rather than constitutional. With the position in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think you described it as being stillborn, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You described it as -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- the still birth of democracy is a term that I have used a number of times. I have used it in regard to the former Yugoslavia. I may have used in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I see various similar processes happening in Yugoslavia and then in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? What do you mean by the term "stillborn" in relation to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you saw, you heard this morning that if I applied Mr. Badinter's criteria to Bosnia and Herzegovina, by the time it was recognised it was non-empirically a state. It was a state in the process of dissolution, to use Mr. Badinter's wonderful phrase. Unfortunately, it got there as a result of 28 elections that were free and fair. It has been one of the tragedies of those of us who have dealt with Yugoslavia for a long time that the country that we saw becoming increasingly open, increasingly democratic, in the 1980s, so much of it after -- which leading to the first free elections has become so much less so as the time has gone past -- this is through the looking glass feeling that one gets if one has been there, that it goes more and more like the -- the various parts of it grow more and more like the Eastern Europe that it had not been since 1965. I think in that sense we could say that most of the elections in Yugoslavia in 1990 were "free and fair", and then we can pronounce them democratic. But, as somebody has said, it does not take one election to have a democracy, it takes at least two, and free and fair -- two free and fair elections in the territories of the former Yugoslavia are hard to find and certainly not to be found in Serbia, Croatia or Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But, even accepting that there is no democracy, if one accepts that, in any of those places, that does not mean to say the state does not exist, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I applied Mr. Badinter's criteria to the existence of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: His definition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, his definition provided criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you told us this morning or it was read to you this morning what that definition was. Perhaps you might tell us the definition that you apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I recalled, Mr. Badinter in the first opinion described 28 a state as a community in a territory subject to organised political authority, and suggested that one needed to look to the Constitutional order to determine the sway of control over the population in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you regard that as being sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I regard it as a quite useful definition. I would be perfectly happy to entertain further definitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I mean, that seemingly could apply to a city council, could it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, if may quote Mr. Badinter, which is all I can do here, he regarded the existence of the state as an empirical question on which recognition was not a deciding factor. I mean, if one looks ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course, at the time he was dealing with the whole issue of recognition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise this, yes. I recognise the recognition. Well, political theorists have written volumes over the definition of the state. I am not a political theorist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you are the one that posited or said you accept this definition, and that is what I am exploring, but you would agree with me, would you not, the fact that you may not exercise control over the whole part of the state or, indeed, that a part of the population of the state is not necessarily represented in the legislative process, is not of itself a factor which would bring about the non-existence or death of a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not of itself necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There are numerous examples of this. 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There are numerous examples of this. I mean, you have Sri Lanka and the Tamils?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you have Sri Lanka and the Tamils.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Cyprus and the Turks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have Cyprus and the Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Israel and the occupied territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are many, many examples, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But nobody suggests for one minute that they are not states, do they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think there is a difference. Certainly Cyprus existed as a single independent state for a period before the government lost control of part of the territory, as did Sri Lanka, of course. So what you have then is an established government that loses control over a portion of the territory -- an established government of a state that can be recognised as an independent state for a while. Bosnia and Herzegovina, as an independent state, however, never had control. In fact, the recognised government of Bosnia and Herzegovina does not have control over either western Herzegovina or the Republika Srspka and it has not, so that this was recognition of a state as a state of a territory, large portions of the population of which rejected inclusion in that state which strikes me -- that is why I have said that recognition of the state had to mean war, because if it is to be realised in the territory that it is recognised, it has to be imposed on the parties that reject it or, having made clear that 28 they reject it, they would also fight to avoid being included within it which is where I believe I ended this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are not suggesting, are you, that the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have control over the whole of the peoples and the whole of the territories of that state for some considerable period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as an independent state, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, but I am asking you the question, they did exercise control over the peoples and territory of that state, did they not, the Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a Republic within Yugoslavia, yes, a control that began to break down, as Yugoslavia was breaking down, but only as a Republic within the control of, within the framework, rather, of Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That framework, of course, had broken down, the framework of SFRY, a considerable period earlier. I think we posited the date 15th May 1991, but you suggested it was even earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was breaking down, yes, and it was breaking for -- its breakdown was repeated, essentially, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We remember that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was also a state recognised by the United Nations. In fact, it was a founding member of the United Nations and a founding Member of the League of Nations before it, but that did not make it empirically a state to Mr. Badinter in December 1991, and if apply his criteria to Bosnia it was not either on the day it was recognised. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the international community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It declared its independence on 6th March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, but here you have the problem with "it proclaimed its independence" but its, "its", existence for one and the competence of those who claim to speak for all of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina were both being challenged by the leadership, the elected leadership, of at least one of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, this represented, as I tried to go through today at some considerable pains, a breakdown of the constitutional structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself as the constitutional structure of Yugoslavia had broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But these factors all go to the determination of whether a place is a state or not, a territory is a state or not, you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a shame Mr. Badinter said that this was an empirical question. I was treating it as an empirical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is also recognised by Croatia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is officially recognised by Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that was one of the clauses in the Dayton Agreement that there is actually a mutual recognition clause, so if that is in the Dayton Agreement (as I believe it is), it would have been effective in December of '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Since 1992 until the present, Bosnia and Herzegovina 28 participates in the international community as a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is accepted by the international community as a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It has embassies that operate around the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It continues to function with government, with President and all the apparatus of a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, having regard to all of that, are you suggesting that it is no longer a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Empirically, the recognised government of Bosnia-Herzegovina has control of approximately 30 per cent of the territory of the state and has never had control over much more than that, and never had control over much more than that when it was recognised as a state. I mean, you know, we can discuss this for a long time. The problem here has been that so many of the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not themselves recognise it as a state. Whether we choose to do so or not, they did not and they were acting in the context of the breakdown of the constitutional organs, the constitutional system, that had existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina up to that time. I mean, I do not know if we could turn it around and propose that the international community could suddenly recognise something as a state and it would thereby be a state. That is actually the logic of your position. I am sure that 28 there is something in the middle, but by Mr. Badinter's criteria, those that were used to say that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in a state of dissolution, so was Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The international community went this way, did it not, because the borders of the state were the borders of the original Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The border is on map. There is a very curious situation if one had been in the former Yugoslavia before all of this. The borders were not usually marked. You did not necessarily know when you crossed from one Republican to another unless you happen to know the place names or there is a change in script. It is not like the United States. If one crosses from New Jersey into Pennsylvania, there is a large sign that says "Welcome to Pennsylvania" and gives you the name of the governor. But there was not anything like that in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So that actually the position that existing borders were being recognised was actually a demand that de facto new borders should be created, because the border was, essentially, meaningless on the ground. It, obviously, has administrative importance, you know, where you pay your taxes and where you vote. But, for other purposes, it was not particularly important. Suddenly the transformation of these administrative borders into, in an attempt to translate, into international borders was, in effect, creating new borders. If these were rejected by the people on the ground, as they were by the Croats 28 of Herzegovina and the Serbs of Bosnia, then what do we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the opstinas of Bosnia-Herzegovina were clearly defined, were they not? People knew where their opstina was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which opstina they lived in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They knew that those opstinas were in a particular Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. I mean, clearly the borders were there as defined as certainly administrative borders. Absolutely. There is no question about it. But did you not have to stop and show your passport which would make it a physical barrier, and that is what would have to be created.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not have stop and show your passport coming into Holland from Germany anymore either, but that does not mean to say the Netherlands is not a state, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, but this is a very curious dynamic because at the same time that the European Community is saying it is perfectly all right to create new physical borders in the Balkans, we are removing borders. That was very odd. I mean, the whole treatment of this by the European Community was very odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it was not only the European Community, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was not only the European Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, the United States of America was certainly involved in all of this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it was just not limited to that. Would you agree with me that the recognition of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 28 United States and by the European Community turned the conflict in that country into an international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An interesting question, Mr. Niemann. Well, it is an interesting question. Let me give you a counter. In early 1991, the Foreign Minister of Italy, Mr. Dimichaelos(?), told the Slovenes and the Croats that, "If you folks secede, you are going to cause a war and we are going to put a wall around Yugoslavia, and when you have stopped killing each other we will deal with you". Now, had that been the stance of the international community, certainly no one would have said that this was an international conflict. If you are saying that the pronunciation by however we define the international community turns a civil war into an international conflict, I suppose that one could well argue that. I suspect it is not going to have much effect on what is motivating the people in a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Maybe not, but you certainly accept it as so, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You certainly accept it as so that the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina turned the conflict, transformed it, into an international conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I do actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I can just ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I know you may be referring to my response to a critic, a letter in the Slavic Review that was written in probably early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am referring to two articles which you wrote. One, The 28 Yugoslav Collapse, National Suicide and Foreign Assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, which I wrote as it was taking place ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- with less time for reflection than one might ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I might just quote what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "With the recognition of the independence of Slovenia and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and their acceptance of the United Nations, the European Community and the United States legally transformed the civil war into international conflict".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I wrote that in approximately May of 1992 and I believe I rethought my composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you have changed your mind on that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have done a bit more research.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about an article you wrote called The Bosnian Debacle? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is a much more resent article, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How recent is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How recent is that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19 -- early '95, early '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Only you say on page 14 of that article: "The legal effect of the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to transform a civil war into an international conflict"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as part of a rhetorical structure, I had not actually done 28 much research on that aspect of it. It certainly was not key to the thrust of either the 1992 article or the 1994 article. One does sometimes put in material that might be viewed as dicta rather than holding in an academic article as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So are you telling us now that this is no longer your view, you do not hold this view any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think I do hold that view any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are there any other views you have had told us about in the course of your evidence that you do not hold to be true any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so. I will stick to the evidence as I presented it. I might remind you that Lord Caines was once asked if he had changed his mind, and he said: "When I obtain new information I change my mind. What do you, sir?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. So it is on the basis of further information, is it, that you change your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Further information and thought. I have been working on this for quite a while, as you, apparently, have had the dubious pleasure of seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might tell us what matters or factors you have taken into account which influence you to change your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this particular point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I looked more carefully at Badinter and I looked at certain references in international law. I am an anthropologist and lawyer specialising in Yugoslavia. I do not pretend to be an international lawyer, but I do research as problems become 28 apparent to me. The problems in this regard had become increasingly apparent to me. I am surprised that you have not cited the opening paragraphs of the article that I published in Radio Free Europe Research in May of 1993, the one called The Partitioning of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1990 to 1993, in which I suggest that how one characterises the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina depends on the definitions that one uses, and this is a subject of debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what you are suggesting is that all the world is wrong when it recognises Bosnia-Herzegovina as being a state, but that you have it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am applying Mr. Badinter's criteria as he stated them. That he changed his criteria after the fact of recognition is something that you might well raise with Mr. Badinter. The province of Bosnia and Herzegovina had remained, that although Bosnia and Herzegovina has now sat at East River in New York for more than four years, the government that sits there does not control, has not controlled, all of the territory, and very large portions of the population reject it entirely. That is a rather different situation and a situation that involves -- that requires looking at the conditions within Bosnia and Herzegovina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is true, Professor, is it not, that the Serbs were much more willing to go to war rather than being incorporated into a state since they controlled most of the guns and much of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And they also perceived themselves as having the most to lose,, although we could also say that the Croats in the territories where they controlled also went to war for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you agree with me when I make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is something that you have said in an article entitled "The Bosnian Debacle" at page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the outbreak of fighting commenced, there were large peace rallies, were there not, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo and in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These demonstrations in Sarajevo were largely stopped as a result of being fired upon (in your words) almost certainly by Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the beginning of April of 1992, Serb forces, including many from Serbia, were attacking Muslim towns in Eastern Bosnia while Croatian forces, including many from Croatia, were attacking Serb settlements in Posavina and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my understanding when I was writing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina spurred further military action by the Serbs because if their incorporation into 28 Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be prevented by voting, it was to be done by force, preferably with large territorial gains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said today when I closed, it seemed to me that civil war was inevitable either to impose the state on those who reject it, or they would go to war to avoid being incorporated into the state that they rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The action, the military action, by the Serbs was extremely aggressive, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has been presented that way to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have presented it that way, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was reporting what I was certainly understanding at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that is ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I provide, I usually provide citations and I am not sure what I am citing, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This does not seem to have a citation here. It seems to be a direct quote from your writings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know it is a direct quote from what I am writing. What I exactly I was citing I am not quite sure. I mean, I am sure I was reporting what was regarded as general knowledge at the time, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will read out precisely what you said and see whether you can agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On page 15 of the article Bosnian Debacle ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be the opportunity, your Honour, that the Prosecutor would present a copy of the writing to Professor Hayden when referring to it so that he can look at the context 28 in which it is?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, would you do that? First, identify the article, if you have not already, and if you have an extra copy, if you are going to read a quote from it, can you give the entire article to Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will identify the article, your Honour. I am fairly sure that the Professor knows what I am talking about. Page 15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy, I cannot actually tell you if this is the version that was published or not because this is a draft in which I say "Forthcoming - The Diplomatic Record", but I know I went through a number of redactions, and I cannot actually tell you that this is the final version as it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you write it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I certainly wrote it and then, you know, I rewrite them as editors comment upon them and I know that this one went through some rewritings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means tell us if there is something there that you do not agree with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you go to page 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you read out that section on page 15 under the heading "The military petition of Bosnia, 1992 to 1993", that whole section there going over to the first sentence in the top page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. "The war was, however, marked by the extreme 28 aggressiveness of the Serbian forces, who had received much support from Serbia and from the Yugoslav National Army, the JNA. Serbian plans for arming Serbs outside of Serbia and for redrawing the borders of Serbia in order to include all Serbs in case of the collapse of Yugoslavia" ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might read it a little slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- I am sorry --- "were rumoured in 1991". Shall I put it up here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It might be a good idea if you did that, and perhaps if you could read it just a little bit more slowly because it has to be taken down in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The war was, however, marked by the extreme aggressiveness of the Serbian forces, who had received much support from Serbia and from the Yugoslav National Army, the JNA. Serbian plans for arming Serbs outside of Serbia and for redrawing the borders of Serbia in order to include all Serbs in case of the collapse of Yugoslavia were rumoured in 1991. The existence of these plans was confirmed by General Veljko Kadijevic, Federal Secretary of Defence until January 1992, in a remarkable book published in Belgrade in 1993, in which General Kadijevic acknowledges that he did not try to defend the integrity of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as he was sworn to do, but rather tried to establish borders for a new Yugoslavia for the Serbian narod". I am not sure what the footnote is, probably to Kadijevic. "In regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kadijevic acknowledges that the JNA in B&H was transformed into 'the backbone of the Army of the Serbian Republic, with complete 28 armament and equipment'. The Serbian Army was staffed primarily by soldiers from B&H".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not wish to say anything about the context in which it appears?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think I was asked by the editor to include something on Serbian plans, so I wrote it in this way, and I think that has been quite clear from Mr. Kadijevic's book. The question, of course, goes to the nature of support and when it was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have relied upon it as a source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Mr. Kadijevic's book, General Kadijevic's book? Oh, yes, as I said, it is a fascinating book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A credible source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will treat it as such, although some people say otherwise, but I treat it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you must have given it sufficient reliability in order to put it in your works, presumably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Surely, I cited it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You would not like to be seen to be relying on unreliable sources, no doubt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that the Serbs took much of the northern region of Posavina in order to secure the vital corridor to their lands in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that corridor had been cut off at the very early part of the war, yes. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am looking, just to assist you, specifically at page 16 in relation to these questions, so just you have it in front of you. About two-thirds of the way down the page: "Both Serbs and Croats took land from the Muslims, although the Serbs took far more than did the Croats", is that right? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, can I read it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You go on to say in this article: "The brutal 'ethnic cleansing' that accompanied these military campaigns turned world public opinion against the Serbs, as the side that was most engaged in brutalising civilians", which picks up on a point that I asked you earlier, I think, about the civilians being most affected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Another one of your articles that I would like to take you to, if I may -- again I will give you a copy of that so that you can look at it while I am asking you questions about it -- did you write an article "Imagined Communities and Real Victims: Self-determination and Ethnic Cleansing in Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did indeed. It is gone through many, many revisions. I am fascinated that you have my drafts!

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to this particular article, in particular I would like to take you to page 4, if I may?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The very last sentence on that page, I asked you some questions 28 about this earlier today ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- it appears in this article perhaps in a clearer way. You say there at the very bottom: "The powerful tool of appealing to local chauvinism was first seized openly by the Serbian leader, Slobodan Milosevic". You go on over the page: "In openly advocating a nationalistic cause, Milosevic rejected one of the basic pillars of Yugoslav communism". Then you go further down: "However, in 1989, in part in response to fears that Milosevic had designs on becoming another Tito, the Slovenian leadership, still communists, adopted a nationalistic political Platform of their own." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. It sounds familiar, but I do not actually see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might go to the top paragraph of page 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I just looked down too far, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You agree with that as a proposition expressed there, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as part of the entire, I think it is not inconsistent with what I have been saying today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Going over to page 6 of the same article, you see there about the middle of the page: "Indeed, it is my argument", page 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. The middle page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might put that on the screen: "Indeed it is my argument" ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I cannot locate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right here. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I am sorry, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, your Honour. "Indeed, it is my argument that the spatial patterning of the war and its terrible ferocity are due to the fact that in some regions, the various Yugoslav peoples were not only coexisting but becoming increasingly intermingled." Then in particular: "In a political situation premised on the incompatibility of their components, these mixed territories were not only anomalous, but threatening, since they served as living disproof of the nationalistic ideologies. For this reason, the mixed regions could not be permitted to survive as such, but their populations, which were mixing voluntarily, had to be separated militarily"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is similar to what I was saying at the end of direct testimony this morning in response to some of the questions from the Judges, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The separation militarily was, at least in part, carried out in perhaps the most ferocious form by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By them all, by them all. I had in mind not simply Bosnia and Herzegovina but the parts of Croatia that were most mixed which, as I said this morning, had not voted for the nationalist parties but had voted for the reformed communists in an attempt to save themselves, and the war was, indeed, about unmixing many of these regions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke in your evidence about the constitutional court examining the Amendments to the Slovenian Constitution and you mention that the Court was not recognised by Slovenia, is that right? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You remember your evidence on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that not only did the Court look at the Constitutions of Slovenia, but indeed all of the Constitutions of the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. As I said, after the 88 Amendments of the federal Constitution all of the republican Constitutions were amended and the federal court was looking at those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that in the final analysis the Court decided that the Constitutions of all of the Republics and provinces, with the exception of Montenegro, contained provisions contrary to the federal Constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, yes. I believe I gave it some greater specificity in the article that you are citing, but I do not actually remember now. I mean, it found different provisions of different Constitutions out of congruity with the federal Constitution, but it was December of 1989 and I do not remember the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think if I remember your evidence correctly you only referred to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, I did. That was the -- we were discussing the Slovenian Amendments at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also referred us to an article contained in Exhibit 46, did you not, Defence Exhibit 46?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I do not know the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might be shown that Exhibit? (Handed) 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This particular newspaper article, I think, was published sometime this year, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of months ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It contains the various views of the Slovenian academics that took part in this discussion in Slovenia that you referred to in your evidence, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the Serb participants as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think in your evidence you made reference to the fact of the various speakers and you took us to parts of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am wondering if you would translate for us, as best you can, the provision, the last paragraph on the first column of the second page, the last paragraph of the first column, the very bottom paragraph there. If you have trouble, if you feel uncomfortable about translating that, please let us know and we can put it on the screen and ask the translators to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is when one begins with the word "nedjutim" or the one that begins "u tekstu".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "U tekstu"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "U tekstu", yes, I will be happy to. It is here. Do you want me to translate it, your Honour, or would you like the translators to do it? I have no problem in doing it, but if you would rather have the translation service do it, I will read it in Serbo-Croatian and they can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps we might do it that way, your Honour, and in that way if you feel more comfortable that way, it is probably the easiest. 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is immaterial to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you are comfortable to translate it, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will make the decision if you two cannot decide. Why do we not have the interpreters translate it for us? OK. It says [In translation] "In the text that follows I will attempt on the basis of my notes to reconstruct the discussion of all the participants in the conversation".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If we can start again and do it much more slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, sorry. Still I hear him very loudly on Channel 4 and he drowns out the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I just do it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think perhaps, your Honour, his voice comes in at first but then it cuts out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We will see if it cuts out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "In the text that follows I shall attempt to reconstruct on the basis of my notes the discussion of all the participants in this interview. By the very nature of things, it was impossible to take note of every uttered word. Nevertheless, the author vouches that the substance or the spirit of what was deliberated about has been recorded authentically." 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. From that, would you say that this is not direct quotes from the speakers, it is merely a reconstruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the way that Professor Markovic presents it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your evidence you spoke of people voting for particular ethnic or national groups -- particularly I am referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and I think you probably had in mind, if you did not expressly say so, the SDS, the SDA and the HDZ in relation to elections in 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You suggested, I think, that people who voted for these particular parties were pursuing or giving their vote to a particular ethnic national cause; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said specifically was that, given the chance to vote as undifferentiated Bosnians, they partitioned themselves into Serbs, Croats and Muslims overwhelmingly, a pattern that has occurred before in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed that is a fair construction that could be placed on a reason for a person voting for one of those particular parties, but there are other motives that people could have, are there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it is not exclusively, people do not exclusively vote or may not have exclusively voted for these parties because of the fact that they wanted to promote nationalism as such. It may have been democracy, might it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on how one defines it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you suggest that the SDS, the SDA and the HDZ represented 28 these minority groups, sorry, these particular national groups, what is the basis of you saying that they had the mandate to so represent them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were the elected representatives of these people. I think you would have been very hard pressed to have found a Serb who voted for the SDA or a Croat who voted for the SDS or a Muslim who voted for the HDZ. It may have happened, but the patterns seem fairly clear. This is how Bosnian elections earlier in the century have been interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it is possible, is it not, that there were Serbs, Croats and Muslims outside of these particular parties who put their vote into other parties, other political parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible and there have been stories that I really do not know much about, that is part of agreements to oust the communists that there were agreements that, for example, Croats in one area would vote for the SDA. But I really do not know the details of this, so I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did nationalistic Serbs discourage other Serbs from voting in the 1992 Bosnian referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, they certainly did not encourage them to do so. There have been reports of some discouragement of some people in some places. However, as I recall, Dr. Gow said in his testimony that most Serbs would have boycotted the referendum in any event, and I agree with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed it is true, is it not, that Serbs who were seen as offering any kind of concessions or whatever to the other groups were viewed as traitors? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the logic of this type of politics which becomes increasingly polarized. One could see this outside of Bosnia, but in Yugoslavia after the late 1980s that compromise was somehow seen as betrayal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In reality there really is nothing in particular to physically distinguish the various ethnic groups as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do the states of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or at least some of them, see themselves as sort of being existing states before the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia came into existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am sorry the state? I believe you may have misspoken. Do you mean Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina? You said the states of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yugoslavia. Did the states of Yugoslavia see themselves as historic states which existed prior to the federation into the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which, once that past, they in effect sprung up again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly Serbia and Montenegro were independent states in 1914. In fact World War I began when the Austro-Hungarian empire using the excuse of the assassination of the Arch Duke in Sarajevo attacked and invaded Serbia. Serbia of course, then Serbia and Montenegro, were incorporated into the first Yugoslavia which was actually called the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes at the end of World War I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about Croatia, did it see itself as an historic state that sprung up after the removal of the Socialist Federal Republic as such? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the Croatian Constitution, the preamble has a really very interesting lesson, a history lesson, on the continuity of the legal identity of the Croatian state which is a matter of, essentially, holy writ to Croatian politicians. However, the Croatia that went into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was a part of the Austro-Hungarian empire and was not regarded as an independent state within the Austro-Hungarian empire. In fact, I do not think there had been an independent Croatian state for many centuries, but I am not a historian and the farther back we go the more bothered I would be by saying anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you say it was in a similar position to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was also incorporated from the Austro-Hungarian empire into the first Yugoslavia. Bosnia and Herzegovina had been incorporated into the Austro-Hungarian empire on a date that I am afraid I cannot specify. It had gone out of the Ottoman empire in 1878 and was a protectorate of Austro-Hungary, but when it was actually annexed into Austro-Hungary I am not sure. Before that there had not been an independent Bosnian state, again for many centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I suggested to you that at least Croatia saw itself as being a state which was in existence and then came back into existence, as it were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, it would not surprise me in the least. I am aware of the claims. One of the early extreme nationalist Croatian political parties was called the Party of Croatian Right, 28 meaning state right, and in fact a party under that name still exists. No, I am quite aware of the position, but I doubt that many non-Croatian historians would accept the conclusion that Croatia was an independent state for many, many centuries before, well, before 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I am not so much concerned about the time, but the understanding that it was historically a state which went into a federation and then emerged from the federation again as an independent state. So, do you agree with me that there is nothing surprising in them seeing themselves in this light?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said that I know that Croatian politicians see themselves in this light. I said that I doubted that many non-Croatian historians with agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that many of the urban Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina desired the continuation of the Bosnian state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would it be your view that the Serbian campaign of terror forced deportation and murder in Croatia in 1991 and Bosnia in 1992, paralleled that waged by the Ustasha, the independent state of Croatia in World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be possible to view it that way. One does go rhetorical on some of these occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if I were suggest that these were ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course it would not. I sometimes respond to editors who request that I include things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, it went all that quick that I do not exactly what article list, but the Prosecutor has asked you to quote page 16 almost at the bottom. I do not know whether this article is still there and whether you could tell us what article it is. Perhaps you would put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think it was that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What I remember was that it was page 16, but it went so quick.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is 16 of the other one I had not seen again today. So it must have been this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you put it on the screen I will be able to recognise it. Yes, Professor Hayden, you stopped quoting three lines from the bottom. Would you please quote the last part as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beginning with "However"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "However, all sides engaged in atrocities against civilians aimed at forcing them to leave their homes. By late 1992 more than 2 million people were refugees within Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Hayden. Another question to you. You have been asked by the Prosecutor, and you referred this morning, to be a consultant to Mr. Panic for, as you said this afternoon, five days. Could you please tell us where Mr. Panic is living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic is a citizen of the United States as well as Yugoslavia and lives and conducts his business in California.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the aim of Mr. Panic was when attending 28 the London conference you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted to end the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, you were asked by the Prosecution on your opinion about the international character of the conflict. Before writing on this subject, did you study the precise distinctions that are made under international law as between the differences, the distinction between internal conflicts and international conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Those were my questions, your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Professor, I had one question that you might help me with. You spoke earlier about the period 1941/1945, and the way in which the various armed forces attacked particular populations. I am not at all clear about what happened to the Muslims in Bosnia during that period. I perhaps understand what happened at the hands of the Ustasha. I am not at all clear as to what happened to the Muslims vis-a-vis the Chetniks and the partisans. Was there any particular pattern, and what part did the Muslims play? Did they form mainly part of the Chetnik forces or of the partisan forces? I assume they formed no part of the Ustasha forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, the inconsistencies of the Ustasha philosophy did not only include the idea that converting Serbs would serve, I suppose, to make them no longer Serbs. The Ustasha also 28 viewed officially the Muslims as being part of the Croat nation. In fact they used the term "the flower of the Croat nation", saying that they had been Croats who had been converted to Islam. The independent state of Croatia included Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Ustasha, I do not believe that the Ustasha conducted campaigns against the Muslims. To the contrary, there were Muslims who were Ustasha and much of the slaughter of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1941 to '45 was conducted by Croats and Muslims. The Serbs were, undoubtedly, the largest victim numerically at that time. Muslims joined the partisans in increasing numbers as the war went on. The partisans were an integrated force. The Chetniks were very hostile to the Muslims, and there were Chetnik massacres of Muslims particularly in eastern Bosnia I believe in the latter stages of that war, but it has been a long time since I have read any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have just a few questions, Professor. Maybe you can help me as a cultural anthropologist. I do not know that I fully understand what that means, but perhaps you can answer some of the questions that I have in my mind. Mr. Orie just asked you a question and he asked you to read from the last couple of lines of an article that you had written and you said that: "However, all sides engaged in atrocities in late 1992 leading to perhaps 2 million refugees." What I want to ask you, it may be a difficult question but try, what do all of these events that we have seen over the last five years, I suppose, in 28 the former Yugoslavia, what do all of these events that transpired with all of the atrocities you have written about and that we have heard about by all sides, what does that tell the world? Is this something unique that happened in the former Yugoslavia, or does this have any relevance to world communities that have multiple ethnic compositions? Particularly you told the Chamber that civil war was inevitable after the referendum, even though in the preamble of the Bosnian-Herzegovina Constitution it, unlike all of the other republics, recognised multiple peoples. It is a long question and perhaps it is not even fair to you, but it is something that keeps going through my mind as I hear all of the experts appear before us and give us all of this information, this very scholarly information, and I say to myself, well, what does that have to do with today and what does that have to do with tomorrow and what does that have to do with other world communities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can attempt to answer this. It is a complicated question and I will start with the first part of it and then you might be able to remind me of the other parts. I should have actually taken notes but I did not. Is all of this unique to Bosnia and Herzegovina or to the former Yugoslavia? The answer to that is clearly no. As I said earlier today, I actually began my career as a scholar of India. I have not seen anything from Bosnia since 1992 that I do not find in reports from the Punjab in 1947, the Punjab being, the position of the Punjab being in many ways between India and Pakistan and with no majority because 28 there was a third community in the Sheiks, in many ways analogous to that of Bosnia in 1992. In an article of mine that that Mr. Niemann did not quote I have actually drawn on this parallel a bit more and do so in other work. I think that when you find the partitioning of mixed regions you would expect to find these types of atrocities. I think that if you look at the events in the early 1920s that involved separating an independent Greece from a post-Ottoman Turkey you would find something similar. You would find similar events on much smaller scales, with the partitioning of Cyprus in 1974. You can find similar events actually with the expulsion of 10 million Germans from Poland and from Czechoslovakia and from Yugoslavia in 1945. The creation of homogenous nation states, more or less, is a very European process in this century. For example, the Poland that was created after World War I was only 65 per cent Polish with very large German and Jewish populations. It is now one of the most homogenous states in Europe. I could give other examples. I would not say, and I would never say, that these processes are inevitable. Quite to the contrary. I try in my work to look at the circumstances in which this type of ghastly partitioning becomes inevitable. I may say, for example, that we can look, as I said earlier today, at India as a multi-lingual, multi-religious, multi-ethnic, in any ways that you may care to look at it state, which is also a functioning democracy, it is possible to do this. It is possible to maintain a functioning democracy in these circumstances, but it 28 requires a great deal of political effort. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, as I said, it might have been possible for Bosnia to have not been partitioned if the people, peoples, if the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina had identified themselves primarily as Bosnians, but they did not, they identified themselves primarily as Muslims, Serbs, Croats and others and they voted that way, whether knowingly or not they elected politicians who proved incapable of maintaining the compromises that were stated in the Bosnian, provided for in the Constitution of Bosnia, but it was in a context in which they were simply following the same political processes that had occurred in the destruction of the political compromises and the constitutional structures that had ordered the Yugoslav Federation. My view of Bosnia is that I say it is inevitable, I said it was inevitable at the time and I would tell you that if you look at -- it is very well attested that Mr. Izetbegovic, among others, did not want the recognition of Slovenia and Croatia before a deal was reached for Bosnia because he knew also what would happen. The demise of Yugoslavia set off, essentially, if I may be metaphorical, an avalanche. The international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina amounted to an attempt to stop an avalanche halfway down a mountain. I do not think it is possible to stop avalanches. I think the point is to prevent them. I would hope we could learn some lessons from this to help us to prevent avalanches. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What lessons can we learn? Particularly, what was the effect of the outside influences, if any? Muslims were 44 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 19 ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- and Croats then were what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs were 31, 32 and Croats about 17.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So you have a sizeable Serb minority, 33 per cent or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A third of the population, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: A third of population who you say fear that if Bosnia-Herzegovina secedes, then they will go unprotected, but they were living within that Republic for whatever number of years that the Republic had existed since World War II I guess. So what was the role then, if any, of outside influences that may have encouraged this feeling that they were not safe within a Republic that seceded from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I understand why you are here to testify and I am not interested in ascribing blame. I heard from Dr. Gow and I heard Mr. Orie say that Dr. Gow had suggested that it was the growth of the greater Serbian nationalism when he was responding to Judge Stephen's question as to why you were here. You are here to tell us another side, perhaps, a different view. So really what I am trying to find out is why. I am still after this "why" and maybe we will not find a why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several outside forces obviously. I personally have always felt that if the international community had put 100th of the effort into preserving the Yugoslavia that did exist that it 28 has put into attempting to create a Bosnia that it was clear to me and it was clear to many others was not going to exist, perhaps none of us would be here. But once Yugoslavia began to collapse like this, it may be that the difference in the way I have looked at things has to do primarily with the fact that I have been looking at the actions of the people and at the political actors and the structures within Bosnia and Herzegovina rather than those from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not see how they were operating in a vacuum. We see Slovenia's Constitution. Let me ask you about the preamble and the Constitution of Serbia.
