You did indicate that the preamble recognised the primacy of the Federal Constitution, but what did it say about, we, the peoples, whereas Slovenia said Slovenes, Croatia Croatian, you were not asked I guess, but what did it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I included it in the box of the Constitution and I think I went alphabetically, Serbia, Republica Srpska, Krajina which was in Croatia and the Republika Srpska are all there. They are all there because the formulations are quite congruent. The justification for Serbia is based -- I do not have the text in front of me, but it is based on the struggle of Serbian narod for its own state, as are the rest of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That was that page we spent so much time trying to see if we could get it in without the whole article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the one, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So the preamble to the Serbian Constitution then says basically the same thing that the Slovenian amendment said and the 28 Croatian amendments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are all congruent structures. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina stands alone saying, we, peoples, mentioning Muslims, Serbs and Croats, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is so, but I would only say that Bosnia and Herzegovina was the one that did not really have -- well, there was the amendment, yes, I am sorry. Yes, you are correct. It was amended in 1990 to drop the working class and all working people and to leave the nations, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Orie, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have one additional question, your Honour, and it relates to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, was the fact that under the former federation there was some protection for all groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina to live more or less safely together, might that be an explanation also of why things changed after the fall down of the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. As someone asked earlier, it may have been Judge McDonald, if Tito had, or Mr. Niemann, I am not sure who, if Tito had suppressed nationalism and certainly it did, then Tito's Yugoslavia, this type of division, could not take place. Of course, there was constitutional provision for equality and non-discrimination and the like, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have additional questions? 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one question. I keep trying. (To the witness): When Slovenia seceded there was not civil war within Slovenia, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Over there was the 10-day border war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What was that? Would you describe that war for me? Did Serbia invade Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The Federal Army attempted to control the borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, yes, the Yugoslavia Army. It was a Federal Army in its structure and its recruits at that time. It goes into that time as a Federal Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So when Slovenia seceded the JNA came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the JNA was there. I mean Slovenia was part of Federal Yugoslavia. Its constitutional job was to defend the country, to control the borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Whether they came in or whether they were there, in any case it was the JNA that engaged with whom in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Slovenian Territorial Defence forces who took control of border crossings. There was not much fighting actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: A few days and that was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then in Croatia, when Croatia seceded there was not civil war, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The secessions of Croatia and Slovenia were simultaneous virtually, and the focus of everything was on Slovenia, on the borders of Slovenia. A senior American diplomat had expressed 28 to me several months earlier when I questioned what would happen when Slovenia secedes, the answer was that the Yugoslav Army will control the border and no one will recognise them. In fact, the Yugoslav Army did not control the border after the 10 days. Then there was a period, as I said earlier today, of this quiescence, the phoney war, for a while which lasted until the late summer and the fall of 1991 when fighting broke out in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That was also the JNA, is that not so, that were either there or came in there to quell the Territorial Defence attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA then became -- I am not a military expert, so perhaps I should not speak on this. My understanding is that the JNA, it was the Army of the Yugoslav Federation. As the Yugoslav Federation was collapsing so was the JNA, and you had apparently a quite chaotic situation in which some officers were defecting, others were not. Remember at this time the Minister of Defence was General Kadijevic who was of a mixed Serb and Croat parentage. The Assistant Minister of Defence was Admiral Stane Brovet who was a Slovene. You had a mixed Officer Corps and yet, you know, one officer who had been in charge of the 5th Military Division of he Yugoslav Army became Croatian Minister of Defence. All sorts of things are happening. Soldiers are leaving. You have extraordinary scenes of marches of mothers, of bus caravans of mothers from Macedonia through Serbia to Croatia to these besieged camps to get their sons out of the army. It was disintegration of so many institutions, including the army. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So war broke out in any case, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: War broke out in Croatia at the time of the secession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the late summer and fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So then what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not very much different, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not so different. It is just that it did not happen until the war in Croatia was largely over. The Yugoslavs were noted for black humour, and one of the black elements of black humour in late 1991 in Bosnia was, you know, why isn't Bosnia involved in the war? The answer was because these are only the semi-finals and Bosnia got a seed in the finals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In 1990 what was the ethnic percentage in Yugoslavia, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, all of Yugoslavia? What was the largest group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will embarrass myself. Certainly the largest group were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: By far I guess?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, certainly, they are the largest group. Yes, far and away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next group is then Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: And after that Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, Slovenes, they are both about 2 million. Yes, 2.1 million Muslims, 1.9 million Slovenes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, what will we do tomorrow? It occurred to me you do not have another witness for this week, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right. As we discussed earlier, it was the intention of the Defence to proceed on the 17th with our first witness of fact. Because of the elections I have no opportunity to bring them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And the problems with your other expert witnesses who will be available at a later time, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I rescheduled them to the last week, to have them all together, that would make sense, instead of mixing them with the witnesses of fact as soon as they are available. We might use the time perhaps, your Honour, because, as I said, we will file this motion on protection. As a matter of fact, we will file it tomorrow morning and perhaps you could hear it on Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Friday at some point we were going to issue a decision in a Rule 61 proceeding that we had and we had scheduled that for 4.30. You are filing the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: First thing tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will that require then argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you think it will be opposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I hope not. I have no reason to believe it will. It is in the sequence of previous requests and I would say there are no new elements involved. So it is more or less the same as 28 what we have already dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it is not to be opposed then there is really no reason for us to discuss it in Chambers. There is another motion, Judge Stephen reminds me, that has been filed, a confidential motion, by the Prosecutor. I do not want to discuss it any more, but you have received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you oppose that motion? Is that something we can talk about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not ready to take a position yet, but we might discuss the matter tonight and we might be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Perhaps tomorrow afternoon. I am concerned about the interpreters. I do not want to keep them hanging and available if we do not need them. What we will do is then to adjourn, just talking with the Registry and Miss Featherstone, we will adjourn until Tuesday. Then we can begin Tuesday. Professor Hayden, you are sitting here listening to all this. Is there any objection to Professor Hayden being permanently excused, unless you are just interested in this you can sit, otherwise is there any objection to Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, you are permanently excused. Thank you very much for coming. We can adjourn until Tuesday at 10 o'clock and you can tell the Registry whether it is necessary to begin in closed session on Tuesday for your motion and, Mr. Niemann, for your 28 motion as well. The two of you will know whether there is going to be opposition. If there is no opposition we may not have to discuss it, but you will resolve that, tell the Registry whether we need to meet in closed session on Tuesday at 10. We will just adjourn until then. We will handle the other matter we needed to handle that does not relate to this case when we need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The decision on our motion on dismissal will be read in court or just handed?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have not actually decided whether we are going to issue a written decision or whether it just will be orally delivered. It would have been ready tomorrow, so perhaps we will do it as a minute entry or we will resume again on Tuesday and then just announce the ruling. But we are still deliberating on that. Any questions? We are missing two days. Let us not do that again. From looking at your new witness list, Mr. Wladimiroff, and the way you prepared it is very helpful, it takes us to October 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That does not include time for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It does include time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you have estimated? They can estimate your cross-examination, Mr. Niemann! They have been with you so 28 long they know how long it is going to take!

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have had some experience now, have we not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is good. Then rebuttal, Mr. Niemann, do you know at this point how long you would need for rebuttal? The time for filing your rebuttal witnesses has not arrived yet. Can you give us any clue at this time, if you can?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is very hard, your Honour, to give an estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But when you file your list then of course we will have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will know then, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because we must finish this case before the end of November, we absolutely must. It looks like we can now because I did not realise that the October 25th date included cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If you would not had suggested that I would have because really it should end indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. We still are concerned though about losing days. So let us handle the time that we have as efficiently as possible. So we will adjourn until 10 a.m. You let the Registry know whether we need to meet in closed session on Tuesday, otherwise it will be in open session on Tuesday at 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Court is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The court adjourned until Tuesday, 17th September 1996). 26 27 28
